en: The Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter One: The Introduction (I). Chapter One: The Introduction.
Homage to the Buddha Śākyamuni. Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling in the Palace of the Dharma Realm, in the sphere of the Tathāgata—a supreme place adorned with the blazing radiance of all kinds of jewels, extending throughout immeasurable worlds.
The place where great radiance is emitted, universally illuminating all;
the dwelling place of immeasurable and skillful distinctions;
the place that is without boundaries and transcends all limits.
It is a place that transcends all realms of the three worlds, a place of accomplishment for supramundane and most excellent roots of goodness;
it is a place of perfect purity, sovereign liberation, and non-obstruction;
it is a place sustained by the spiritual power of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
It is the sphere of activity of immeasurable multitudes of bodhisattvas;
it is the sphere of activity of immeasurable multitudes of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth;
it is the place where great joy and bliss are ultimately fulfilled within the great dharma-realm.
It is the place that ultimately bestows benefit upon all sentient beings;
the place free from all defilements of affliction;
and the place adorned by the sustaining power of all Buddhas, far removed from all Māras and adversaries.
It is the place where the intent of the Great Dharma proceeds and is clarified;
it is the realm of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the Great Vehicle;
it is the place of the bliss of the great liberation of entering emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
The Bhagavān dwells in such inconceivable and sovereign places as this, adorned with the great jewel lotus-kings of immeasurable multitudes of merit.
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, have awakened to what is well-awakened; they are free from dualistic conduct and have reached the realm of signlessness.
They practice the conduct of all Buddhas and attain the universal equality of all Tathāgatas, reaching the destination that is without obstruction.

They are able to reach the wheel of Dharma of non-retrogression, the invincible realm, and the inconceivable essence; they reach the equality of all three periods of time, pervade all worlds with their bodies, and arrive at the state of certainty regarding all dharmas.

They are able to reach the conduct of all ultimate wisdom; they are able to reach the state of doubt-free knowledge of all dharmas; they have attained all non-discriminative bodies; they are able to answer all the questions of bodhisattvas regarding wisdom; they are able to reach the further shore of non-dual conduct; they are able to reach the place of the Buddhas’ non-differentiated liberation-wisdom;
they are able to reach the boundless and centerless samādhi, whose sphere is as vast as the dharma-realm and as ultimate as space;
and they will remain until the end of the future, together with immeasurable assemblies of śrāvakas—whose minds are well-tamed and...
These sons of the Buddha have well attained liberation of mind, well attained liberation through wisdom, and well attained pure precepts;
they grant joy to those who seek the Dharma, have accomplished great learning, maintain great learning, and are fully endowed with great learning;
they are skilled in what they contemplate, skilled in what they speak, and skilled in what they do; they have well attained—
Possessing all swift *prajñā*, having well-attained all rapidly moving *prajñā*, and having well-attained all sharp and penetrating *prajñā*;
endowed with the three types of clear knowledge (*traividya*), seeing the foremost Dharma, attaining ultimate practice, and being able to effect purification;
they receive from great donors the fulfillment of accomplishments and the ultimate tranquility of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*).
They have attained accomplishment, are patient and gentle, well-receive the Buddha’s teachings, and are able to practice according to what has been taught.
At that time, a great assembly of immeasurable bodhisattvas came together from immeasurable and diverse buddha-fields—
all these bodhisattvas dwell in the great state of all that is sought and are ultimately able to grasp it.
The unsurpassed Great Dharma attains the mind of equality toward all sentient beings, abandons all conceptual discriminations,
and subdues all demons and adversaries through such discrimination. It leaves behind all objects of contemplation belonging to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
and fully possesses the joy and bliss of the flavor of the Great Dharma, transcending the five...
They had attained the stage of non-retrogression from fear, the reality-body of the One Vehicle was manifest before them,
and they were able to extinguish the fears of all sentient beings; together with such an assembly of bodhisattvas— unspeakable, inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, and incalculable in number.

Chapter Two: The Inquiry of the Noble Bodhisattva Subhapṛccha (1). At that time, the Bhagavat was surrounded before and behind by a great assembly of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of asaṃkhyeyas, and he was teaching the profound Dharma for the sake of the bodhisattvas.

At that time, among the great assembly there was a noble Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva named Suvicikṣaṇa (Good Questioner), who sat within the gathering and, relying upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) that is ineffable and devoid of dualistic characteristics, addressed the noble Bodhisattva Ghanavyūha (Deeply Secret Liberation), saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!
It is said that all dharmas are non-dual.
Regarding the statement that all dharmas are non-dual: what constitutes "all dharmas," and what is meant by "non-dual"?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gambhīravyūhavimukti addressed the Bodhisattva Suṣṭhapraśna, saying: "Good son,
regarding what is called 'all dharmas,' there are two kinds."
What are these two? First, conditioned phenomena; second, unconditioned phenomena. Good son!
"Conditioned phenomena are neither conditioned nor unconditioned;
unconditioned phenomena are neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Subhāṣtapraśna.
“O Son of the Buddha!
How is it that conditioned phenomena are neither conditioned nor unconditioned?
And how is it that unconditioned phenomena are neither conditioned nor unconditioned?”
The Bodhisattva Gambhīravyutthita said:
"Good son! That which is called 'conditioned phenomena' is merely the Tathāgata’s teaching through names."
Regarding what is called the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma through names: it is merely the discrimination of linguistic expressions that is termed "teaching the Dharma. Good son!

If teaching the Dharma were merely the discrimination of linguistic expressions consisting of names, it would not be so; rather, it is formed by the gathering together of various names and linguistic expressions.
Therefore, it is said that they are not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Good son!
That which is called "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) is merely the substance of words.
"Good son! Even if one were to depart from both the conditioned and the unconditioned, that dharma would likewise be so. Good son!"
Although there are no words, the matters spoken are not empty.
O Son of the Buddha!
What are these matters such that they are said not to be empty?
What is called the noble ones' knowledge is the noble ones' vision; the noble wisdom knows the vision of the noble ones, which is realized beyond words.
Yet, wishing to explain that ineffable Dharma, one speaks of the conditioned and the unconditioned by relying on conventional signs.
Good son! That which is called "unconditioned" is merely the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma by means of names;
that which is the teaching of the Dharma by means of names is a characteristic of discrimination.
The characteristic of discrimination is precisely the characteristic of speech. Good son!
The characteristic of speech is the phenomenon that is the collection of names.
The collection of names is a false phenomenon;
that which is a false phenomenon constantly lacks such an essence, and the various conceptualizations of names do not constitute anything real, being merely the mark of speech.
Therefore, I say that it is not non-conditioned. Good son,
what is called "conditioned" is merely a name.
If one were to depart from conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, it would be the same for that [person].
Son of good family!
Yet, those words are not spoken without a basis.
"Good son! What is that thing which is said to be known by noble wisdom and seen by noble wisdom?
It is the dharma realized through ineffability."
"Because it is realized through wordlessness, it is called non-conditioned.
The Bodhisattva Subhāṣita asked:
"O Son of the Buddha!"

How is it that those phenomena, which are realized through the ineffable and known and seen by noble wisdom, are described by means of the language of "conditioned" and "unconditioned" for the sake of explaining that dharma which is realized through the ineffable?
The Bodhisattva Gambhīravyūhamukta said: "Good son!

It is like a magician or a magician’s apprentice who stands at a crossroads, gathers grasses, wood, branches, leaves, tiles, and stones in one place, and displays various feats produced by magical arts—namely, elephant, horse, chariot, and infantry troops; as well as mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, coral, amber, musaragalva, agate, wealth, grain, silks, and all manner of objects from storehouses—and thus demonstrates these various diverse things."
"Good son! There are foolish and ignorant ordinary people who, upon seeing or hearing of those things, do not know them to be grasses, trees, tiles, or stones, and give rise to this thought:

'Truly these elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, coral, amber, musaragalva, agate, wealth, grain, silks, treasuries, and other such items exist, because they are perceived by direct observation.'"
That foolish person, having seen and heard this, immediately adopts it for practice, regarding it as ultimately true and all else as false.
Good son! That person must further seek the supreme among the supreme dharmas.

“Good son! Furthermore, there are those with wisdom who are not deluded; when they see elephants, horses, and the like, they know them to be of the nature of grass, wood, tiles, stones, and so forth.”
Upon seeing and hearing this, that person gives rise to such a thought:

"These various elephants, horses, chariots, and so forth that I see are not real; they are produced by illusion. These false appearances of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, along with these various diverse matters, deceive the human eye."

That wise person, regarding what they have seen and heard, does not take it to be real nor does they cling to it; nor do they take this to be ultimately real while considering the rest to be false. Rather, they understand it as a conventional designation for the sake of meaning and grasp those words. Such a person need not further contemplate superior dharmas.
"Good son! It is just the same for ordinary beings who have not yet attained the supramundane wisdom of the noble ones.
Being ignorant and deluded, ordinary beings do not know, as it truly is, the ineffable Dharma; yet upon seeing and hearing conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, they give rise to such thoughts:
"There exist these conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, as I have seen and heard.

For this reason, that person, according to what they have seen and heard, ultimately grasps them with attachment as real; and according to what they have seen and heard, they practice accordingly—thinking, "This alone is ultimately real, all else is false"—that person must further investigate the superior Dharma.

“Good son! Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are not foolish; having seen the True Reality (satyadharma) and attained the supramundane wisdom of the noble ones, they are able to know all phenomena as they truly are. They realize the ineffable, true essence of phenomena, yet upon seeing and hearing conditioned and unconditioned dharmas, such beings give rise to this thought:
‘Regarding what has been seen and heard, there are no such dharmas as names for conditioned or unconditioned things.’”
Again, he reflects:

"These discourses on the conditioned and the unconditioned arise from the modes of activity of false discrimination; they are like illusory phenomena that delude the intellect, giving rise to various names and marks for the conditioned and the unconditioned."

That person understands that they do not grasp things through seeing and hearing by thinking, "This alone is true; all else is false"—they employ words merely to clarify that meaning—and such a person need not further contemplate superior dharmas.

“Good son! Such matters as these—known by the wisdom of the noble ones and seen by the vision of the noble ones—are realized beyond words. Yet, desiring to realize that ineffable Dharma, one speaks of the names and characteristics of the conditioned and the unconditioned.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gambhīrārthavimukta spoke these verses:
"The profound meaning is beyond words; The Buddhas teach non-duality."
Fools rely on ignorance and cling to dualistic conceptual proliferation;
they travel long upon the worldly path, coming and going without rest,
and are born among the animals because they have departed from the ultimate truth.

Chapter 3: The Inquiry of the Noble Bodhisattva Dharmodgata (1) Chapter Three: The Inquiry of the Noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata At that time, the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, relying upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as it truly is—which transcends all characteristics of the realms of discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) of every world—addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

I recall past lives, even further back than those past lives: beyond this world, after passing through worlds as numerous as the sands of seventy-seven Ganges Rivers, and further beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers, there was a buddha-field named Renowned World (*Yaśas*). In that land dwelt a buddha named Vimalagati Tathāgata.
At that time, while wandering to transform sentient beings, I went to that world.

There, I saw a non-Buddhist teacher residing in a certain place, with seventy-seven thousand disciples gathered around him, contemplating all phenomena according to the characteristics of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-lakṣaṇa*).

Those various non-Buddhists together sought the characteristics of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-lakṣaṇa), weighed the characteristics of the ultimate truth, and contemplated the characteristics of the ultimate truth; yet, though they examined them, they did not perceive the characteristics of the ultimate truth. Consequently, they gave rise to diverse thoughts, diverse views, and diverse attachments. They established diverse factions and initiated disputes, contending with one another through the power of speech and uttering unwholesome words. Having thus mutually confounded one another, they rose up and departed in dispersion.
"Bhagavān! At that time, I immediately gave rise to this thought:
'How rare it is that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, appear in the world!'"

Because they rely upon the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world, they are now able to see and hear the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-lakṣaṇa*) that transcends all worldly spheres; they are able to realize the ultimate reality, perceive the ultimate reality, and witness the cessation of all phenomena.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, saying:
"Dharmodgata! So it is, so it is."
I have awakened to the ultimate characteristic that transcends all worldly realms; having thus awakened, I speak of it for others, show it to others, reveal it to others, and establish this Dharma.

Why is this? For the sake of the noble ones, I teach the Dharma realized within my own person; for the sake of ordinary beings, I teach the realm of vitarka and vicāra, which is mutually known by all.
Dharmodgata! You should now understand, based on this meaning, that what is called "transcending the spheres of all worlds" is the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, Dharmodgata!

When I speak of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is a realm that transcends all characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) are what constitute the realm of characteristics.
Likewise, when I speak of the ultimate truth, it is a realm beyond words; discursive thought and investigation are what constitute the realm of verbal expression.

Dharmodgata! I say that being free from all verbal expressions is the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*), as well as names and words, are the characteristics of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Likewise, I say that being free from all disputes is the characteristic of the ultimate truth; discursive thought, investigation, names, and words are the characteristics of dispute.

Dharmodgata! Based on this characteristic of meaning, you should now know that the realm beyond the conceptualization and discernment of all worlds is the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Dharmodgata!

For example, suppose there is a person who throughout their entire life eats only bitter and pungent flavors and delights in bitter and pungent flavors; that person would be unable to know, unable to perceive, unable to measure, and unable to believe in the sweet and delicious flavors of rock honey, *āpāpaka* sugar, and the like.

“Dharmodgata! There are people who, throughout the long night, have believed in and delighted in sensual pleasures, being attached to sensual desires; their inner minds are scorched by the fire of sensual desire, so that their bodies cannot know, cannot awaken to, cannot measure, and cannot believe in the pleasure of freedom from all forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles that is devoid of sensual desire.”

“Dharmodgata! There are people who, throughout the long night, have faith in the pleasure of conceptualization and delight in conceptualization; they are unable to know, unable to awaken to, unable to measure, and unable to believe in the non-conceptual pleasure of internal tranquility.”

“Dharmodgata! Suppose there is a person who, throughout the long night, delights in the pleasure of seeing, hearing, perceiving, and cognizing, and practices with faith and delight; such a person is unable to know, unable to awaken to, unable to measure, and unable to believe in the internal tranquility that is free from seeing, hearing, perceiving, and cognizing.”

“Dharmodgata! Suppose there is a person who, throughout the long night, has delighted in the notion of a self and the characteristics of a self, practicing with faith and pleasure; that person would be unable to know, unable to awaken to, unable to measure, and unable to believe in the joy of non-self and non-mine found in Uttarakuru.”

“Dharmodgata! A person who possesses such discursive thought and investigation cannot know, cannot awaken to, cannot measure, and cannot believe in the mark of the ultimate truth (paramārtha) that is free from all discursive thought and investigation.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“I speak of the Dharma realized by the body, The supreme realm beyond words,
Free from the signs of vitarka, vicāra, and contention— The ineffable ultimate truth.”

Chapter Four: The Inquiry of the Noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvishuddhamati (1) At that time, the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvishuddhamati, relying upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) which transcends the characteristics of identity and difference, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The World-Honored One has well expounded the rare and wondrous Dharma, the ultimate truth—the subtle, most subtle, and profound meaning that transcends the characteristics of identity and difference—namely, that which is difficult to realize.
“World-Honored One!

I recall that in the past, while at a certain place, I saw various bodhisattvas dwelling on the stage of practice through faith gathered together in one location, contemplating whether conditioned phenomena and the ultimate truth are one or different.”
Some bodhisattvas say: "The characteristics of conditioned phenomena are different from the ultimate truth.
Furthermore, other bodhisattvas speak as follows:
"It is not that conditioned phenomena are different from the ultimate truth," yet he says:
"Conditioned phenomena are not different from the ultimate truth."
Furthermore, there were bodhisattvas who gave rise to doubt and conceived a contrary view, saying:
"Among these bodhisattvas, which one speaks the truth?"
What is false speech?
What is the method of practice for right mindfulness?
And what is the method of practice for wrong mindfulness?
"World-Honored One!
When I see those bodhisattvas, I think to myself:
'These sons of good family are all deluded; they lack skillful wisdom, do not well understand the Dharma, and have fallen into wrong thoughts.'"

"Why is this? Because they are unable to know that conditioned phenomena are subtle and signless, transcending the signs of identity and difference, and possessing the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Viśuddhamati, saying:
“Suvihitamatī! It is so, it is so.
All those sons of good family are indeed foolish and lack skillful wisdom; they do not know the true Dharma and have fallen into wrong thoughts.”

Why is this? Because they are unable to know the subtle characteristics of activity that transcend the characteristics of identity and difference, which are the characteristics of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Why is this?

“Suvihitamatī! If conditioned activity were not distinct from the characteristic of the ultimate truth, then all foolish ordinary beings would likewise perceive the ultimate truth within their very bodies as ordinary beings; they would also attain the bliss of that unsurpassed, pure nirvāṇa, and they would likewise attain that anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

“Suvimalamati! If conditioned phenomena were not distinct from the characteristic of the ultimate truth, then when one perceives the ultimate truth, one would perceive the characteristics of conditioned phenomena.”
If the characteristics of conditioned phenomena were themselves the bonds of characteristics, then those characteristics would be fetters, and liberation would be impossible.
If one who perceives the true reality were not free from the bondage of characteristics, they would neither attain liberation nor be released from the fetters of affliction;
because they would not be free from these two kinds of bondage, they would not attain the bliss of unsurpassed, pure nirvana, nor would they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

“Suvishuddhamati! For this reason, foolish ordinary beings do not perceive the true reality; yet it is not by means of this very body of an ordinary being that they attain that unsurpassed, pure nirvāṇa, nor is it by means of that very body of an ordinary being that they can attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
Therefore, one who perceives the true reality should not perceive those conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) modes of existence as being either identical or different.

Consequently, for such a person, when perceiving the modes of the conditioned and the mode of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the meaning of identity and difference does not establish itself as either identical or different.
Suvihitamatī! You should know this:

if those bodhisattvas claim that conditioned practice and the characteristic of the ultimate truth are either identical or different, those bodhisattvas lack right mindfulness; they possess wrong mindfulness.

"Furthermore, Suvimalamati! If the characteristic of conditioned phenomena and the characteristic of the ultimate truth were not distinct, then just as conditioned phenomena fall into the category of defiled characteristics, the characteristic of the ultimate truth would likewise fall into defilement."

Suvihitamatī! If the characteristics of conditioned phenomena were different from the characteristics of the ultimate truth, then all conditioned phenomena would not be identical to that ultimate truth.
Suvimalamati! The ultimate truth does not fall into the defilement of any afflictions; for this reason, it can be said that conditioned phenomena and the ultimate truth share the same characteristic.
Therefore, Suvimalamati! You should not say that the characteristics of conditioned phenomena and the ultimate truth are either identical or different. Furthermore, Suvimalamati!

If the characteristic of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) were not distinct, then the ultimate truth would not be distinct from all conditioned phenomena; likewise, all these conditioned phenomena would also not be distinct from the characteristic of the ultimate truth.

However, those conditioned phenomena are distinct from the ultimate truth—if they were not distinct, then practitioners who see, hear, perceive, and know the characteristics of conditioned phenomena would have no need to further seek the unsurpassed, supreme Dharma.

“Suvimalamati! If the characteristics of conditioned phenomena were not distinct from the characteristic of the ultimate truth, then conditioned phenomena themselves would have to be designated as having the characteristic of being selfless and lacking intrinsic nature, which is the characteristic of the ultimate truth.”

“Suvihitamatī! Furthermore, there is another fault: namely, at one time [perceiving] distinct and differing characteristics—thinking, ‘This is a defiled characteristic; this is a purified characteristic.’”

Therefore, Suvishuddhamati! The characteristic of the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is different from the characteristic of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), yet it is not non-different from the characteristic of conditioned phenomena.
For this reason, those who practice according to reality, having seen, heard, sensed, and known, further seek the supreme Dharma.

Because one knows conditioned phenomena as they truly are, one attains the designation of the ultimate truth of non-self; yet, there is no simultaneous differentiation between the two characteristics of defilement and purity.
Therefore, apart from those conditioned modes of activity and the mode of the ultimate truth, the sense of being neither identical nor different cannot be established. "Suvishuddhamati!
Those bodhisattvas spoke thus:

"If one were to say that the characteristics of conditioned phenomena and the characteristics of the ultimate truth are neither identical nor different, those bodhisattvas would not be said to speak well."
“Suvishuddhamati! You should know that those bodhisattvas are not said to practice with right mindfulness according to reality; rather, this is called wrong mindfulness. Suvishuddhamati!”
For example, the whiteness of a conch shell cannot be said to be identical to it, nor can it be said to be different from it;

likewise, the golden-yellow color of a lute, its wondrous sound, the fragrance of agarwood, the pungent taste of long pepper, the bitter taste of harītakī, the sweet taste of sugarcane, the softness of tūla-cotton, ghee, and even clarified butter (sarpis)—these cannot be said to be identical to them, nor can they be said to be different from them.
Suvihitamatī! Thus, the essence of all conditioned formations and their characteristic of impermanence cannot be said to be identical, nor can they be said to be different;
all that is tainted and the characteristic of suffering cannot be said to be identical, nor can they be said to be different.
Within all phenomena, there is no characteristic of a self; it cannot be said to be identical, nor can it be said to be different.
The defilements of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the characteristic of non-quiescence, cannot be said to be identical, nor can they be said to be different.
“Suvihitamatī! Thus, all conditioned phenomena and the characteristic of the ultimate truth cannot be said to be identical, nor can they be said to be different.”

“Suvishuddhamati! Thus, I have attained the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) that is subtle, extremely subtle, profound, very profound, difficult to realize, and exceedingly difficult to realize, which transcends the characteristics of identity and difference; having realized it, I explain, reveal, manifest, and establish it for others.”
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke these verses:
“The conditioned realm and ultimate truth are characterized by the departure from identity and difference.
To discriminate between identity and difference is the delusion of one who lacks right mindfulness.”
“Those people are bound by signs And bound by afflictions;
By practicing vipaśyanā And śamatha, they attain liberation. Chapter Five:

The Inquiry of the Venerable Subhūti (1) At that time, the Blessed One, relying upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)—which is of a single flavor and equal flavor in all places—addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
“Subhūti! Do you know how many sentient beings within the realm of all sentient beings rely upon a self and pride when they speak of what I have attained? Subhūti!”
"Do you know, among all the realms of sentient beings, how many sentient beings are free from selfhood and pride when they speak of what I have attained?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"Within the realm of sentient beings, I have truly seen very few who, free from the conceit of 'I' and 'mine,' speak of what they have attained.
World-Honored One!

I have, however, truly seen immeasurable, incalculable, and ineffable numbers of sentient beings within the realm of sentient beings who, relying on the conceit of 'I' and 'mine,' speak of what they have attained."
“World-Honored One!
As I recall, in the past I was dwelling in a certain forest hermitage. At that time, many bhikṣus were residing around me on all four sides.”
"Bhagavān! At that time, I saw those bhikṣus gathering in one place after the sun had set, grasping at various characteristics of dharmas and expounding upon the truths they had realized."
“World-Honored One!
There are bhikṣus who grasp at the characteristics of the aggregates (skandha) and declare them to be the Dharma of realization;

there are bhikṣus who see the characteristic of the arising of the aggregates and declare it to be the Dharma of realization; there are bhikṣus who see the characteristic of the cessation of the aggregates and declare it to be the Dharma of realization.”
Some bhikṣus teach the dharma of the cessation of the aggregates; some bhikṣus teach the dharma of the direct realization of the cessation of the aggregates;

some bhikṣus, perceiving the characteristic of entering, declare it to be the dharma of realization; some bhikṣus, grasping the characteristic of the twelve links of dependent origination, declare it to be the dharma of realization;
and some bhikṣus, grasping the characteristic of the arising of formations, declare it to be the dharma of realization.

There were some bhikṣus who took the characteristic of the truths (*satya-lakṣaṇa*) and taught it as the dharma of realization; some bhikṣus took the characteristic of the cause of the truths (*satya-hetu-lakṣaṇa*) and taught it as the dharma of realization;
some bhikṣus took the characteristic of the knowledge of the truths (*satya-jñāna-lakṣaṇa*) and taught it as the dharma of realization;

some bhikṣus took the characteristic of detachment from the truths (*satya-viveka-lakṣaṇa*) and taught it as the dharma of realization; and some bhikṣus took the characteristic of the realization of the truths (*satya-sākṣātkriyā-lakṣaṇa*).
It is taught as the Dharma of realization: there are some bhikṣus who take the characteristics of the cultivation of the truths as the Dharma of realization;

there are some bhikṣus who take the characteristics of the dharmas of the elements as the Dharma of realization; there are some bhikṣus who take the characteristics of the elements themselves as the Dharma of realization;
there are some bhikṣus who take the characteristics of the various elements as the Dharma of realization; and there are...
Some bhikṣus take the sign of the immeasurable realm and declare it to be the dharma of realization; some bhikṣus take the sign of the cessation realm and declare it to be the dharma of realization;
and some bhikṣus take the sign of the realization of the cessation realm and declare it to be the dharma of realization.

“In this way, monks, some grasp the characteristic of the four foundations of mindfulness and declare it to be the Dharma of realization; some monks grasp the characteristic of the four foundations of mindfulness and declare it to be the Dharma of realization; some monks grasp the characteristic of the four foundations of mindfulness as their respective antidotes and declare it to be the Dharma of realization; some monks grasp the characteristic of the practice of the four foundations of mindfulness and declare it to be the Dharma of realization; some monks grasp the characteristic of practicing so as to give rise to the four foundations of mindfulness that have not yet arisen and declare it to be the Dharma of realization; some monks grasp the characteristic of practicing so as not to lose the four foundations of mindfulness that have already arisen and declare it to be the Dharma of realization; and some monks grasp the characteristic of practicing so as to increase and broaden the four foundations of mindfulness that have already arisen and declare it to be the Dharma of realization.”

"In this way, monks, taking up right effort, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the path, for the sake of producing what has not yet arisen, for its stability, for its non-forgetfulness, and for its increase and expansion, they grasp at signs and declare it to be the realization of the Dharma."
“World-Honored One!
I saw those bhikṣus give rise to this thought:
‘These bhikṣus, being attached to the mark of a self and grasping at the mark of self-conceit, speak thus as their realization.’”
Why is this? Because they are unable to know the characteristic of the single flavor and equal flavor of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Therefore, World-Honored One!
I had this thought:

"It is rare, truly rare, that the World-Honored One has appeared in the world, skillfully expounding the supreme Dharma—the ultimate truth which is of one flavor and equal flavor in all places—subtle, profound, difficult to awaken to, and difficult to know; how much more so could those of external paths ever attain understanding?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is, so it is.
Just as you have said, the Dharma realized by me is subtle, extremely subtle; profound, most profound, and supremely profound; difficult to awaken to, and extremely difficult to awaken to.”

The ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), characterized by the single taste and equal taste in all places, is that which I have realized; having realized it, I reveal, expound, demonstrate, fully disclose, and manifest it for others.
Why is this? Subhūti!

That which is called the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; the arising of formations through causes and conditions; the sphere of the true truths; the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of awakening, and the path—Subhūti! [all these are likewise empty.]

I say that within the five aggregates, the pure contemplation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-lakṣaṇa*); it is the characteristic of the single flavor and equal flavor of all aggregates, elements, bases, foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, awakenings, and the path.

Subhūti! Based on this meaning, you should now understand that in all places there is the single taste, the equal taste, which is the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

A bhikṣu who practices according to reality knows, as it truly is, that one aggregate (skandha) is, according to the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), the dharma of selflessness (anātman). Regarding the remaining elements—the sense bases (āyatana), the factors of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), the formations (saṃskāra), the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), the right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), the bases of power (ṛddhipāda), the faculties (indriya), the powers (bala), the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), and the path (mārga)—he does not further observe them separately as being the suchness (tathatā), the ultimate truth, or the dharma of selflessness. Rather, relying on conformity to suchness and abiding in the non-dual dharma, he realizes the mark of the ultimate truth as a single flavor and equal flavor in all places.

Subhūti! Relying on this meaning, you should understand it thus: that which is called the single flavor, the equal flavor, is the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

Just as there are distinctions among those aggregates, elements, and sense bases; the factors arising from conditions; the applications of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, awakenings, and paths—if the dharma of suchness, the ultimate truth, and selflessness were to possess distinct characteristics, then the dharma of realization that is suchness, the ultimate truth, would also have a cause.
If it had a cause, it would have to arise from a cause;
if it arose from a cause, it would necessarily be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
If it were conditioned, it could not be called the ultimate truth;
if it is not the ultimate truth, one must further seek the ultimate truth.

Subhūti! Therefore, the dharma of selflessness within the ultimate truth of suchness is not born from causes, nor is it a conditioned dharma; yet it is not that it is not the ultimate truth, nor does one seek a further ultimate truth for the sake of that ultimate truth.

Rather, at all times and forever, whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the nature of dharmas (dharmatā) abides eternally, the essence of dharmas (dharmakāya) abides eternally, and the realm of dharmas (dharmadhātu) abides eternally.
Subhūti! Based on this meaning, you should understand that the characteristics of all these dharmas are of one taste, an equal taste, the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya). Subhūti!

For example, although there are infinite varieties of distinctions, the characteristics of form are signless, without conceptual differentiation, and without disparity; in all places, they are of a single flavor and a single essence, equal to space.

“Subhūti! All dharmas have distinct characteristics in their own nature, yet in all places they possess the single taste, the equal taste, which is the characteristic of the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“The Tathāgata should teach the Dharma as having the single flavor of all things, not departing from the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); to perceive distinctions therein is conceit.

Chapter Six: The Inquiry of the Noble Bodhisattva Vipula-mati (1) At that time, the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vipula-mati, relying upon the characteristics of the mind, addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One! Regarding what the Tathāgata has said— that Bodhisattvas are well-versed in the profound and secret dharmas of mind (citta), thought (manas), and consciousness (vijñāna)— World-Honored One,
how does a Bodhisattva become well-versed in these profound and secret dharmas of mind, thought, and consciousness?”
“World-Honored One!
For what reason does the Tathāgata say that bodhisattvas well understand the profound and secret dharmas of mind, thought, and consciousness?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vighuṣṭamatī, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Viśālamati!
That you are now able to question the Tathāgata regarding such a profound meaning.”
"Vipula-mati!
You are able to provide all sentient beings with the requisites for peace and happiness, causing them all to be fully satisfied.
Vipula-mati!"
Out of compassion for all devas and humans, and for their great peace, happiness, and benefit, you have been able to ask me about such a matter.
Excellent, Viśālamati!
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
I shall explain for you the profound and secret meaning of mind, thought, and consciousness. "Vipula-mati!

Within the cycle of birth and death across the six realms of existence, what kinds of sentient beings—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation—undergo the acquisition of bodies, the production of bodies, and the growth of bodies?

Initially, there arises the mind containing all seeds; through different combinations, it develops distinctions and expands extensively, accomplishing its results by relying upon two kinds of grasping.
What are these two kinds?
The first is grasping based on the faculties of form and mind; the second is grasping based on the accumulation of linguistic proliferation and conceptualization regarding non-discriminative marks.
O Widely Wise One!

In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), consciousness arises dependent on two kinds of grasping (*upādāna*); in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it does not arise dependent on those two kinds of grasping.
"O Vipaśyanā-mati! That consciousness is called the *ādānavijñāna* (appropriating consciousness)."
Why is this? Because that ādāna-vijñāna appropriates this body as its corresponding basis.
O Vipaśyanāmati!
It is also called the ālayavijñāna.
Why? Because it dwells with attachment within that body and because it is associated as a single entity.
Vipula-mati!
It is also called "mind" (citta). Why is this?
Because that mind serves as the basis for the increase of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects.
"Vipula-mati! Depending upon that ādāna-vijñāna, the sixfold group of consciousnesses arises—namely, the groups of visual, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness."
Vipula-mati!

If a single object appears before one, a single body of consciousness arises; that is, the non-conceptualizing mental consciousness (manovijñāna) arises simultaneously with the visual consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna).
Vipula-mati!
If two, three, four, or five objects appear before one, the five groups of sensory consciousness arise, and the non-conceptual mental consciousness arises simultaneously with them.
"Viśālamati! It is like flowing water: if a single condition arises, a single wave is produced; if two, three, or even many conditions arise together, then many waves are produced."
"Viśālamati! Furthermore, that flowing water is never interrupted. Moreover, Viśālamati!"

For example, in a stainless, pure, and bright mirror, if the conditions for one image appear before it, one sees that single image; if two, three, or many images appear, one is able to see all those various images in their entirety.
"Vipula-mati!
That clear mirror is not different from those various images. Vipula-mati!"

Just as with flowing water or reflections in a clear mirror, depending upon and being sustained by the *ādāna-vijñāna*, if the conditions for a single visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*) are present, then that single mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) simultaneously perceives the object together with that visual consciousness.
Vipula-mati!

If the fivefold causal conditions for the five groups of sensory consciousnesses manifest simultaneously, the non-conceptual mental consciousness then apprehends objects at the same time as the five sensory consciousnesses.

“Viśālamati! In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in knowledge based on the Dharma, correctly and as it truly is understands the profound and secret dharmas of mind, thought, and consciousness.”
"Vipula-mati!
Furthermore, the Buddha does not say that bodhisattvas and others are those who well understand and know the profound and secret dharma of mind, thought, and consciousness.
Vipula-mati!"
If a bodhisattva does not perceive an internal or external *ādāna*, and does not perceive the *ādānavijñāna*, they are able to know things as they truly are;

they do not perceive the *ālaya*, they do not perceive the *ālayavijñāna*, and they do not engage in conceptual proliferation regarding the mind; they do not perceive the eye, they do not perceive forms, they do not perceive visual consciousness; they do not perceive the ear, they do not perceive sounds, they do not perceive auditory consciousness; they do not perceive the nose, they do not perceive odors, they do not perceive olfactory consciousness; they do not perceive the tongue, they do not perceive tastes, they do not perceive gustatory consciousness; they do not perceive the body, they do not perceive tangibles, they do not perceive tactile consciousness—O Vipaśyanāmati!

The Bodhisattva does not perceive an internal or external mind, does not perceive internal or external phenomena, and does not perceive an internal or external mental consciousness; he is able to know them as they truly are.
O Vipaśyanāmati!
I say that such Bodhisattvas are well-versed in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
"Vipula-mati!
For this reason, I say that a bodhisattva should know the profound and secret dharmas of mind, thought, and consciousness.
Vipula-mati!"
"When a bodhisattva has thus understood the profound and secret nature of mind (citta), thought (manas), and consciousness (vijñāna), I declare that such a person is a true bodhisattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The various types of ādāna-vijñāna Are able to give rise to all phenomena."
"I have spoken the analogies of water and a mirror; I do not speak them for the foolish.
*Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, Scroll One; *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Indian Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Seven: The Inquiry of the Noble Bodhisattva Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha (Part Two). Chapter Seven: The Inquiry of the Noble Bodhisattva Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha.
At that time, the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha, relying upon the characteristics of all dharmas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One has said that bodhisattvas are well-acquainted with the characteristics of dharmas.
World-Honored One!”
Regarding the bodhisattva who skillfully knows the characteristics of all phenomena: what is meant by "skillfully knowing the characteristics of all phenomena"?

World-Honored One, by knowing how many kinds of phenomena does a bodhisattva come to be called one who skillfully knows the characteristics of all phenomena? And why does the Tathāgata say that a bodhisattva skillfully knows the characteristics of all phenomena?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha!”
It is well that you are now able to ask the Buddha about this meaning.
Forest of Merit!
You are capable of providing all sentient beings with the requisites for peace and happiness, causing them all to be fully satisfied.
Guṇakānanavatī! You are able to have compassion for all humans and devas, bringing them great peace and great benefit, that you are able to ask me about such a meaning as this.
Excellent, excellent! Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha!
Listen now with single-minded attention, listen well; I shall speak for you.
“Guṇakāśyapa! All phenomena possess three kinds of characteristics. What are these three?
These are the characteristic of false conceptualization, the characteristic of causal conditions, and the characteristic of the ultimate truth.
Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha! What is the characteristic of false conceptualization?
That which is called the essence of the dharmas taught through names and signs, as well as their various characteristics, names, functions, meanings, and so forth.
Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha! What is the characteristic of the causal conditions of all dharmas?

What is called the twelve links of dependent origination means that this dharma arises in dependence upon that dharma; that is to say, with ignorance as a condition, there are volitional formations, and so on, until the arising of this entire mass of great suffering.
Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha!
What is the ultimate characteristic (*paramārtha-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena?

It is the essence of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena. By practicing with right mindfulness and practicing with a sincere heart, the bodhisattvas realize the non-dual dharma; having realized that dharma, they eventually attain the accomplishment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Guṇakāśa! It is like a person who has a film over the eye; this is a fault of the visual consciousness. Guṇakāśa!”
False conceptualization is likewise.
Forest of Merit!

It is, for example, as if there were someone with a cataract in the eye who sees the appearance of hair-tufts, ropes, and sesame seeds, manifesting before him in colors such as blue, yellow, red, and white.
Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha!
The characteristics of causes and conditions are likewise thus.
Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha!

For example, suppose there is a person whose eyes are pure and free from turbidity, having been cleared of the defect of cataracts; with such eyes, one perceives the objective realm of its own nature without giving rise to delusion.
Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha!
The characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is likewise so. "Guṇakāśyapa!

For example, if one places pure vaidūrya glass within blue pigment, it produces the light of a great indranīla mani-jewel from that indranīla blue; the indranīla blue and the light of the great indranīla mani-jewel appear before them, and deluded sentient beings mistake it for a real jewel."

Guṇākara! When that body of pure lapis lazuli is placed within a red substance, the radiance of a red padma-maṇi jewel immediately appears before one, causing deluded sentient beings to mistake it for a red gem.
Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha!
When that body of pure vaidūrya is placed within green surroundings, the light of green maṇi jewels immediately manifests before them, deluding sentient beings into thinking it is a green gem.
Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha!
When that body of pure lapis lazuli is placed within yellow [pigment], there immediately appears before one the radiance of golden maṇi-jewels, which deludes sentient beings into thinking it is gold.
Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha!
Just as there are various different colors within that pure lapis lazuli,

so too should you understand that within the characteristics of other-power causes and conditions, the essence of false discrimination— consisting of names, phrases, and habitual perfumings— is likewise.

“Guṇakāśyapa! Just as when that pure vaidūrya is the color of indranīla or mahendranīla, it appears in various forms such as gold and other jewels due to red, green, and yellow hues, thereby deluding sentient beings who all take them for real jewels.
Guṇakara! In this same way, you should know that within the characteristics of dependent origination, the false discrimination of names and phrases is likewise so. Guṇakara!
Just as that body of pure white lapis lazuli is, so too should one understand the causal conditions of other powers.
O Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha!

Within that very body of pure lapis lazuli, there is no blue of Indra, nor the great blue of Indra; there is no such precious substance as blue gems, red, green, or golden gems. At all times and for all eternity, it is devoid of all such precious substances.

“Guṇākara! Within those very characteristics of the causal conditions of other-power, you should understand that the entities of those names and phrases of false discrimination do not exist at any time, nor ever, as corresponding [to reality].”
Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha!
One should understand that dependent origination corresponds to conceptual differentiation based on names and signs.
Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha!
By clinging to names and appearances based on false causes and conditions, one perceives the causes and conditions of other-power (*paratantra*). "Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha!
By clinging to the marks of false discrimination based on the causes and conditions of other-power, one perceives the mark of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)."
Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha!

When a bodhisattva is able to know those characteristics of causal conditions as they truly are, this is knowing the characteristic of false conceptualization; at that time, the bodhisattva is said to be able to know that all phenomena are without characteristics.
Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha!

If a bodhisattva understands the characteristics of the dharma of causes and conditions, and having understood all dharmas of causes and conditions as they truly are, is able to understand the defiled characteristics of all dharmas as they truly are;
and having understood the defiled characteristics of dharmas as they truly are, is able to understand the characteristic of the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
Having known the characteristics of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) as they truly are, one can know the characteristics of pure phenomena as they truly are.

"Guṇākara! If a bodhisattva, within the phenomena that arise through the conditions of other-power, can know the signless nature of phenomena as it truly is, and having known it as it truly is, remains far removed from defiled phenomena; [he shall attain liberation]."
Having become free from defiled phenomena, one attains the realization of all pure phenomenal characteristics. Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha!

A bodhisattva is able to know, as they truly are, the characteristics of false phenomena, the characteristics of dependent origination through other-power, and the characteristic of the ultimate truth (paramārtha), which is signless (animitta). They are able to know, as they truly are, defiled characteristics and pure characteristics, the characteristics of phenomena free from defilement, and the realization of pure phenomena.
Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should thus skillfully know all dharmas.
For this reason, the Buddha says that a bodhisattva mahāsattva skillfully knows all dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Knowing all phenomena as they truly are, One immediately abandons the characteristics of defiled phenomena;
Having abandoned the characteristics of defiled phenomena, One realizes the pure Dharma."
"Not observing the faults of the conditioned, nor the harms of indolence and negligence;
with all phenomena ever immovable, one who is free from signs is called a Bodhisattva.

Chapter Eight: The Inquiry of the Noble Bodhisattva Paramārthasiddhi At that time, the noble Bodhisattva Paramārthasiddhi, relying upon the ultimate characteristic of the absence of intrinsic nature, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!
While I was alone in a secluded place, a thought of reflection arose within me, and I had this thought:”

"The Tathāgata has taught in various ways the self-nature and characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), namely, the knowledge of the characteristics of arising and ceasing; he has taught that one should abandon such conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) that arise from the causes and conditions of the sense bases (*āyatana*);
he has likewise taught the self-nature and characteristics of the truths (*satya*), namely, the knowledge of their realization and cultivation;

and he has taught the self-nature and characteristics of the elements (*dhātu*), including their various distinct characteristics, their various elemental characteristics, and their immeasurable elemental characteristics."

Thus have been explained the intrinsic natures of the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and the path; as well as their respective antidotes and modes of cultivation, whereby those not yet arisen are brought into being, and those already arisen are further increased and expanded.

The World-Honored One further taught: "All phenomena are originally without substance; all phenomena are originally unarisen; all phenomena are originally unceasing; all phenomena are originally quiescent; and all phenomena are by their very nature in nirvāṇa."
“World-Honored One!
For this reason, I ask the Tathāgata about this matter: with what intention did the Tathāgata speak thus?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Paramārthasiddhi, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! You have accomplished the ultimate truth!
That you are able to contemplate with such right mindfulness and give rise to this discernment is well done.”
He spoke again:
"Excellent! You have accomplished the ultimate truth!"
It is well that you are now able to ask the Buddha about this matter. Why is this?

It is because you seek the peace and happiness of all sentient beings, the security of all sentient beings; it is because you desire to benefit all sentient beings and bring peace and security to all devas and humans that you ask about this matter.
Siddhārtha! Listen with a single-minded focus:

for what reason do I say that all dharmas are from the beginning without essence or characteristics, that all dharmas are from the beginning unarisen, that all dharmas are from the beginning unceasing, that all dharmas are from the beginning quiescent, and that all dharmas are from the beginning in nirvāṇa?
“Siddhārthasatya! It is based on the threefold absence of intrinsic nature in all phenomena that I have made this statement: that all phenomena lack an intrinsic nature.”
What are these three? They are:

the characteristic of all phenomena being without intrinsic nature, the characteristic of the essence of non-arising, and the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) being without intrinsic nature.
This is the accomplishment of the ultimate truth!
That all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) refers to their various conceptualized characteristics. Why is this?
Because those phenomena are described according to names and signs and do not possess an intrinsic nature; therefore, I say they lack intrinsic nature.
Siddhārtha! What is the essence and characteristic of the non-arising of all phenomena?
It is that all phenomena lack an essence and characteristic.

Why is this? Because those produced phenomena depend upon the causal conditions of other-power (*paratantra*) and do not possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); therefore, I say that their essential nature is non-arising.
This establishes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
What is the characteristic of the non-substantiality of the ultimate truth?
It is the perfection of the ultimate truth!

Regarding the characteristic of the non-substantiality of the ultimate truth: all phenomena are fundamentally without a substance of arising; therefore, I say that all phenomena lack an intrinsic nature, because they arise in dependence upon causes and conditions, and because they rely upon the non-substantiality of the ultimate truth.
Why is this? Because it accomplishes the ultimate truth!
Among all phenomena, that which is the pure aspect of contemplation—I declare that to be the characteristic of the ultimate truth.

“Siddhārthasatya! Because one observes purity within the characteristic of other-power (paratantra-lakṣaṇa), I therefore say that the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) has no intrinsic nature (svabhāva-lakṣaṇa).”
"O you who have realized the ultimate truth!
All dharmas lack the characteristic of being established; therefore, I say that this ultimate truth has no intrinsic nature or characteristic. Why is this?"
O you who have realized the ultimate truth!
All phenomena are without self and lack the characteristics of a self; therefore, I say that all those phenomena lack an intrinsic nature or characteristic.
O you who have realized the ultimate truth!
Therefore, those dharmas are designated by names based on the absence of intrinsic nature; for this reason, I say that the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) has no characteristic of intrinsic nature.
This, O Accomplished One in the Ultimate Truth!
Just as flowers in the sky have no intrinsic nature or characteristics, so too do all phenomena lack intrinsic nature or characteristics.
Therefore, I say that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature or characteristics; such is the nature of phenomena, and it should be understood thus.
“Siddhārthasāgara! It is like the various forms and images created by illusion; likewise, all phenomena produced by causes and conditions lack intrinsic nature and characteristics.
Therefore, I say that all dharmas are devoid of intrinsic nature and characteristics.”
Excellent, O you who have realized the ultimate truth!
It is likewise that the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) has no intrinsic nature or characteristic.
Therefore, I say that the ultimate truth has no intrinsic nature or characteristic.
O you who have realized the ultimate truth!
Just as the appearance of flowers in the sky is designated by a name despite lacking any substantial essence or characteristic,
so too is it with the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), which likewise lacks any intrinsic essence or characteristic.
O you who have realized the ultimate truth!
It is because these three kinds of dharmas lack intrinsic nature and characteristics that I say all dharmas are devoid of intrinsic nature and characteristics.
Furthermore, O you who have realized the ultimate truth!

My intention is based on the fact that characteristics lack intrinsic nature; thus I say that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. Those phenomena are originally unarisen, those phenomena are originally unceasing, those phenomena are originally quiescent, and those phenomena are originally in a state of nirvana.
Why is this? Because it establishes the ultimate truth!
If all phenomena lack an intrinsic nature or characteristic, then those phenomena do not arise.
If a phenomenon is not born, that phenomenon does not perish;
if it neither perishes nor is born, that phenomenon is originally quiescent;
if a phenomenon is originally quiescent, that phenomenon is originally pure.
If a phenomenon is originally pure, that phenomenon is originally in nirvāṇa.
If this is so, there is not even the slightest phenomenon within it that can be extinguished to enter nirvāṇa.
O you who have realized the ultimate truth!
Therefore, it is based on those characteristics that my intention explains that those phenomena lack an intrinsic nature; for this reason, I say that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen.

"Furthermore, Parameśvara! That which is the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is designated based on non-self (anātman); therefore, because my intention relies upon the ultimate truth which lacks any essential nature or characteristics, I declare that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen."
Why is this? Because it accomplishes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)!

It is named by means of the dharma of selflessness (*anātman*) according to the ultimate truth; therefore, it is called the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) which lacks the characteristic of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*). At all times and for all eternity, the essence of all dharmas is eternally abiding—namely, the unconditioned essence—which is free from association with all afflictions (*kleśa*).
If a phenomenon exists at all times and for all eternity, abiding within the very essence of that phenomenon, it is neither born nor extinguished because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
If a phenomenon is unconditioned, that phenomenon is primordially quiescent;
if a phenomenon is primordially quiescent, that phenomenon is primordially in *nirvāṇa*, because it is free from association with all afflictions and poisons.

Therefore, it is by virtue of the ultimate truth (paramārtha) that the dharma is designated as "selfless" (anātman). I teach that all dharmas lack an intrinsic nature (svabhāva); all dharmas are originally unarisen, all dharmas are originally unceasing, all dharmas are originally quiescent, and all dharmas are originally in a state of nirvāṇa.

“Siddhārthasādhaka! Within the realm of sentient beings, all living beings do not know and do not perceive the distinctions in the essential nature of phenomena through false conceptualization; they likewise cannot know the distinctions in the essential nature of phenomena arising from the causal conditions of the other-power (paratantra), nor do they see the distinctions in the essential nature of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya). For this reason, I teach that these three kinds of phenomena lack the characteristic of intrinsic nature.”
O you who have realized the ultimate truth!

Yet all sentient beings falsely discriminate regarding the essential nature and characteristics of phenomena, the nature of dependent origination, and the nature of the ultimate truth; they falsely discriminate regarding the nature and characteristics of names, the teachings on causal conditions, and the teachings on the ultimate truth.
O accomplished one in the ultimate truth!

All sentient beings speak in such and such ways and experience in such and such ways, relying on the mind of names, relying on the conforming mind, and relying on the mind that employs names; they rely on those discriminations of the essence and characteristics of names, and cling to the essence of other-power, the essence of causes and conditions, and the essence of the ultimate truth.

“Paramārthasiddhi! By clinging in such and such ways, one falsely clings to the essence of dependent phenomena through the conditions of such and such clinging. Based on those conditions, the essence of dependent phenomena arises in future lives, becoming the defilement of afflictions, the defilement of karma, and the defilement of birth. One wanders through the six realms—namely, the destinies of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, asuras, devas, and humans—suffering for a long night and unable to escape the bonds of the suffering of saṃsāra.”
“Pariniṣpanna-paramārtha!

For all those sentient beings who have not planted roots of goodness, who are unable to purify all their karmic offenses, who cannot achieve the power of various roots of goodness, who do not have much faith in the Dharma, and who do not accumulate the karma of merit and wisdom—for them, I teach that all phenomena are unarisen.”

When those sentient beings hear me explain that conditioned formations arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions, they come to know that all phenomena are impermanent, non-eternal, unreliable, and subject to constant change and cessation; thus, regarding all conditioned formations, they give rise to a mind of alarm and fear, and a mind of detachment.

Having given rise to a sense of awe and fear, and having developed a mind of renunciation, those sentient beings cease practicing unwholesome dharmas and cultivate wholesome dharmas. Those who cultivate wholesome dharmas rely on the causes of wholesome dharmas; those who have not planted roots of goodness plant various roots of goodness; those whose karmic offenses are not purified purify their karmic offenses; and those whose faculties are not matured are able to bring them to maturity. By the power of those matured roots of goodness, they are able to have great faith in the Dharma; those with great faith in the Dharma are able to accumulate the treasury of merit and wisdom.
"O you who have realized the ultimate truth!
Although those sentient beings have planted roots of goodness, even to the point of being able to gather the treasury of all merit and wisdom, they have realized the ultimate truth!"

Yet those sentient beings do not know, as they truly are, the essence of those dharmas arising from causes and conditions, their characteristic of non-arising, and the ultimate truth of the characteristic of non-substantiality; because they do not know them as they truly are, they are unable to develop revulsion toward all conditioned formations and are unable to distance themselves from them.

Therefore, all those sentient beings do not attain liberation from the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), the defilement of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*), and the defilement of birth (*janma-saṃkleśa*).
"O you who have accomplished the ultimate truth!"

For the sake of those sentient beings, the Tathāgata again teaches that Dharma—namely, that causes and conditions lack intrinsic nature and that the ultimate truth lacks intrinsic nature—in order to cause those sentient beings to give rise to a mind of weary detachment toward conditioned formations, so that they may attain liberation from the defilement of afflictions, the defilement of karma, and the defilement of birth.

When those sentient beings hear what I have taught, they will give rise to right faith regarding the characteristic of non-arising of all phenomena, regarding the false conceptualizations of all phenomena, and regarding the absence of intrinsic nature and characteristics within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). They will contemplate those phenomena and realize them as they truly are. Within the power of others (*paratantra*), they will not give rise to attachment or false conceptualizations regarding the intrinsic nature and characteristics of phenomena; rather, they will know that these are merely designated by the function of names, merely designated by following the function of names, and that those various afflictions are merely designated by following the function of names.

Therefore, all those sentient beings are able to extinguish the various signs of external causal conditions and, by relying on the power of wisdom in the present life, sever all future causal conditions.
Therefore, by relying on those causes and conditions, right view is able to bring about detachment from all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*);

having become weary of and detached from all conditioned formations, one attains right liberation, remaining far removed from the defilement of karma, the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa*), and the defilement of birth.
“O Accomplisher of the Ultimate Truth!
Beings of the śrāvaka nature rely upon this path and this dharma to attain the nirvāṇa of a śrāvaka;
beings of the pratyekabuddha nature do likewise, relying upon this path and this dharma to attain the nirvāṇa of a pratyekabuddha.”
It is the same for sentient beings with the nature of the Buddha-vehicle: by relying on this path and relying on this Dharma, they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and accomplish the ultimate truth!
Therefore, I speak of a single path of purity for śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.
It accomplishes the ultimate truth!
There is only this one path of purity; there is no second. It is based on this intention that I speak of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
“Siddhārthasādhaka! Within the realm of sentient beings, it is not that there are no beings of various dispositions with soft, medium, or superior faculties. Siddhārthasādhaka!”

As for those of the śrāvaka-nature who abide in quiescent extinction, even if all the Buddhas exert their full power to teach and transform them, they cannot cause them to sit at the site of enlightenment and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Because they have achieved the ultimate truth!

For their own nature is fundamentally narrow and inferior; they are consistently deficient in the mind of compassion, consistently terrified by all forms of suffering, and due to this lack of compassion, they consistently abandon the benefit of sentient beings.
O you who have realized the ultimate truth!

If one is single-mindedly afraid of suffering and single-mindedly avoids all conditioned activities, that person distances themselves from benefiting sentient beings and distances themselves from the work of being able to deliver all sentient beings.
Therefore, I say that such a person cannot realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; I call them a "śrāvaka of cessation.
"You have attained the ultimate truth!"
Regarding those śrāvakas who have generated the bodhicitta, I declare them to be bodhisattvas. Why is this?

Because such bodhisattvas first abandon the afflictive obscurations (kleśāvaraṇa) to attain liberation through wisdom (prajñā-vimukti), and subsequently abandon the cognitive obscurations (jñeyāvaraṇa) to attain liberation through mind (citta-vimukti). These bodhisattvas are the first to be transformed by the Tathāgata; they attain liberation based on their own personal benefit.
Therefore, I say that such a person is a bodhisattva of śrāvaka lineage. "Siddhārthika!

Within my well-expounded Dharma, within the well-suited Dharma, within the well-disciplined Dharma, within the well-purified Dharma, and within the pure Dharma, I have not erroneously taught various characteristics of phenomena based on various natures."

Siddhārtha! Therefore, based on these three kinds of dharmas that lack intrinsic nature and characteristics, the Buddha’s intention was to teach the *sūtra* teachings of provisional meaning, namely: that all dharmas are originally unarisen, originally unceasing, originally quiescent, and originally in *nirvāṇa*.

"Pariniṣpanna-paramārtha! If there are sentient beings who have planted all kinds of supreme roots of goodness, purified their karmic offenses, perfected their faculties, have great faith in all dharmas, and have well accumulated the wisdom of all roots of goodness—those sentient beings, upon hearing my voice of Dharma, will be able to know it as it truly is. Those sentient beings will believe in my Dharma and believe in my meaning; through the observation of wisdom, they will be able to awaken to it as it truly is. By relying on the power of practicing in accordance with that realized Dharma, they will swiftly attain ultimate *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Based on those all sentient beings who are able to give rise to a mind of reverence toward my body and speak thus:
"This is the Perfectly Awakened One; he knows all phenomena; for this reason, he is named the Worthy, the Perfectly and Fully Enlightened One."

“Paramārthasiddhi! If there are sentient beings who have not planted all superior roots of goodness, who cannot purify all sinful karma, who cannot bring all roots of goodness to maturity, who do not have great faith in the Dharma, who lack the superior mind, who have not accumulated the treasury of merit and wisdom, whose nature of upright mind is such that they cannot discern what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma—namely, which dharmas are to be adopted and which dharmas are to be abandoned—but instead act with attachment based on their own mental views, then even though those sentient beings hear my Dharma, they will still not know the underlying intention with which it was spoken.”
Yet those sentient beings, having faith in my Dharma and revering my Dharma, shall speak thus:

"I believe the sūtras spoken by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, which possess extremely profound characteristics, correspond to emptiness, are difficult to see and difficult to realize, whose forms cannot be realized, which are subtle and more subtle than the most minute, and which are the domain of the wisdom of the wise; I cannot understand the meaning of the sūtras that the Tathāgata has taught."
He remained silent and, with faith, spoke these words:

"The bodhi of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is profoundly deep; the essential nature and characteristics of all phenomena are likewise profoundly deep. These are known only by the Buddhas; they are not within my sphere of experience."

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, preach various teachings according to the diverse faiths of sentient beings; while the wisdom known by the Tathāgatas is like the ocean, my knowledge and vision are like the water in a cow’s footprint.

Therefore, if sentient beings can with a sincere heart receive and uphold, copy, preserve after copying, read and show to others, make offerings to, explain to others, constantly recite, and rejoice in giving to others these sūtras, yet they are unable to practice them according to reality within them, it is because they do not know my profound intention and because they have not awakened to it.
O you who have accomplished the ultimate truth!
Because those sentient beings rely upon him, their merit and wisdom increase and reach fulfillment; furthermore, he causes their immature minds to attain maturity.

“Pariniṣpanna-paramārtha! Furthermore, there are sentient beings within the realm of sentient beings who are unable to plant any of the various roots of goodness, and even unable to accomplish the karma of merit and wisdom. They lack a straightforward mind and lack a straightforward intention; yet those sentient beings know what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, what is to be taken up and what is to be abandoned. Through their own intelligence, they give rise to views regarding what is to be taken up and what is to be abandoned. When these sentient beings hear the profound Dharma I have taught, they do not understand my intent; for this reason, they do not know the Dharma as it truly is.”
Because they do not know the Dharma as it truly is, they are unable to awaken to and know all phenomena;
their attachment to the meaning upon hearing sounds is likewise so.
For this reason, all those sentient beings speak these words:

"All dharmas are without intrinsic nature; all dharmas are originally unarisen, all dharmas are originally unceasing, all dharmas are originally quiescent, and all dharmas are originally in a state of nirvana."

Yet those sentient beings, relying on and following this view, give rise to false views regarding all phenomena; they fall into false views by perceiving that all phenomena lack characteristics, because they see all phenomena as being without characteristics.

Because they perceive that all phenomena lack the characteristic of non-existence, they slander all phenomena as being non-existent—namely, the characteristics of false conceptualization, the characteristics of the essential nature of dependent origination, and the characteristics of the essential nature of the ultimate truth.
Why is this? Because it accomplishes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Based upon the essential characteristics of that other-power and causal conditions, and based upon the essential characteristics of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), there exist the characteristics of names.
O Accomplisher of the Ultimate Truth!

If sentient beings see the essential nature and characteristics of causes and conditions, or the characteristics of the ultimate truth, and declare them to be "without characteristics" (*animitta*), those sentient beings slander the characteristics of conventional designations and names. Therefore, I say that those sentient beings slander the three kinds of characteristics.
“Pariniṣpanna-paramārtha!
