Those sentient beings give rise to the perception of phenomena within that which is non-existent as phenomena, and give rise to the perception of meaning within that which is meaningless; they rely upon non-existent phenomena as their support for phenomena, and rely upon meaningless things as their support for meaning.”
O Accomplisher of the Ultimate Truth!

Those sentient beings, relying on my teaching of the Dharma, increase their wholesome qualities; yet, they grasp what is not the ultimate meaning as being the ultimate meaning, and thus their wisdom does not increase.

Those whose wisdom does not increase are separated from all wholesome dharmas; regarding sentient beings who hear the Dharma, they maintain these teachings by taking what is non-meaningful to be meaningful, thereby falling into false views. Those sentient beings grasp at the characteristics of dharmas where there are no dharmas, and the characteristics of meaning where there is no meaning.

Because they grasp at non-existent dharmas as being dharmas, and at what is not the true meaning as being the true meaning, all those sentient beings rely on wrong views and are thus separated from all wholesome dharmas.
"One should know that this is the accomplishment of the ultimate truth!"
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who hear the Dharma from those people of wrong views and speak these words:
"All phenomena are without essence; they are neither born nor extinguished; they are quiescent and nirvana."
Filled with alarm, fear, and dread, they will say:
"This is not the word of the Buddha; it is what Māra has spoken.
For this reason, those sentient beings of wrong views will slander the sūtras, speak against the sūtras, and revile the sūtras, declaring them to be non-Dharma.
Furthermore, those sentient beings, because of that slander of the Dharma, incur immeasurable offenses and accomplish immeasurable, most evil karmic deeds. "Siddhārthasāgara!

For this reason, I say that those sentient beings who slander the Dharma perceive no dharmas and have no reliance on the meaning when teaching the Dharma based on its meaning; they accomplish immeasurable, most evil karmic deeds and cause many other immeasurable sentient beings to likewise generate much karmic offense."

“Paramārthasiddhi! If there are sentient beings who have not planted roots of goodness, whose sinful karma is not purified, whose physical actions are not matured, who largely lack faith in the Dharma, who are unable to accumulate those merits and wisdom, who lack a straightforward mind, and who do not follow a straightforward mind—yet, relying on their own views and false wisdom, they discriminate between what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, claiming ‘this Dharma should be accepted’ and ‘this Dharma should be rejected’—then although such sentient beings hear my Dharma, they do not grasp my intent, they do not give rise to faith, and furthermore, they are unable to know the meaning of what I have taught as it truly is.”

Therefore, all those sentient beings conceive the notion of "Dharma" regarding what is not Dharma, and the notion of "meaning" regarding what is not meaningful; they cling to what is not Dharma while conceiving the notion that it is Dharma, and they cling to what is not meaningful while conceiving the notion that it is meaningful, saying:
"This is not the word of the Buddha; this was spoken by Māra."

Because they understand in such a way through their false wisdom, they slander all dharmas, do not accord with all dharmas, revile all dharmas, and treat all dharmas with contempt; they interpolate false teachings into the True Dharma, for the purpose of destroying the sūtras, subverting the sūtras, causing the sūtras not to be practiced, and preventing the sūtras from being taught, while conceiving thoughts of enmity toward those who have faith in the sūtras.

Those sentient beings already possessed immeasurable karmic offenses and heavy obstructions; furthermore, by slandering the Dharma and slandering others, they further increased their immeasurable karmic obstructions. The fundamental offenses at the root of those obstructions cannot be fully described, let alone the additional offense of slandering the Dharma.

They will fall into the great hells with no prospect of escape; even if one were to speak of their lifespan for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, it could never be fully exhausted.
“Pariniṣpanna-paramārtha!
I have now well expounded these various dharmas, well demonstrated and well purified them, and well explained the various different faiths and various different views of sentient beings.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The essence of dharmas does not arise; it is primordially quiescent, unceasing, and by its very nature in nirvāṇa. For this reason, I say they are eternal."
The three kinds lack intrinsic nature; the ultimate truth is without intrinsic nature.
If one can understand my intention, that person attains liberation.
Through the single path of Dharma, all sentient beings proceed toward liberation.
Therefore, the Dharma of the Single Vehicle is taught with distinctions according to what is heard.
Sentient beings are infinite; for the sake of their own bodies, they seek nirvana.
The Tathāgata is most rare and extraordinary, bringing peace and security to all sentient beings.
"If one realizes the untainted realm, Which is equal and devoid of dualistic characteristics,
And accomplishes all the meanings of Buddhahood, That person is free from afflictions. At that time,
the Bodhisattva Siddhārthasatya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Rare, World-Honored One!

Unprecedented and unheard of before is what the Tathāgata has spoken—so subtle, extremely subtle; so profound, extremely profound; so difficult to realize, extremely difficult to realize; the intentional meaning of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is hard to know.”
“World-Honored One!
I understand the meaning and intent of what the Tathāgata has taught:

namely, that the realm of discrimination exists based on the conditioned characteristics of discrimination; within the context of names, the intrinsic nature and marks of that aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) are called ‘superior marks,’ which are to say: the arising of the aggregate of form, the cessation of the aggregate of form, detachment from the aggregate of form, and the knowledge of the aggregate of form.”
Therefore, the Tathāgata, relying on those dharma-characteristics, declares that all those dharmas are without intrinsic nature.
"World-Honored One!
That realm of discrimination—relying on the mode of activity of that realm of discrimination—is the characteristic of other-power."

Therefore, the Tathāgata, relying upon those dharmas, declares that all dharmas are unarisen and that all dharmas lack intrinsic nature; furthermore, relying upon those same dharmas, he speaks of the ultimate truth as being without the characteristic of intrinsic nature.
“World-Honored One!
I understand the meaning of the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One:

namely, that based upon those objects of discrimination, there is the false discrimination of the conditioned modes of activity; this is precisely the characteristic of that very false discrimination.”

The absence of such characteristics is precisely the characteristic of their lack of intrinsic nature; the dharma of the characteristic of lacking intrinsic nature is selflessness, and the characteristic of the pure contemplation of *tathatā* is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, the Tathāgata, relying upon the ultimate truth, declares that all those dharmas are characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature.
“World-Honored One!
Just as it is with the aggregate of form, so it is with the remaining aggregates;
likewise, it is so for the twelve bases and the eighteen elements—each individual base and all phenomena are also thus.”
“World-Honored One!
I understand the meaning of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata:

namely, that within the realm of conceptual differentiation, there is the false conceptualization of the characteristics of conditioned formations, which is what is called the Truth of Suffering. One knows that the Truth of Suffering relies upon names; it is through the false conceptualization of its own essential nature and its superior characteristics that it is spoken of. Based on this, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas have no essential nature or characteristics.”
“World-Honored One!
That which relies upon the objects of discrimination and depends upon the conditioned modes of activity of discrimination is called the characteristic of causal conditions (nidāna-lakṣaṇa),
World-Honored One.”
Therefore, I say that I understand the meaning of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata. Why is this?
World-Honored One!

That very conceptualization of objects arises based on the characteristics of false activity and the conceptualization of various dependencies; yet those characteristics of false conceptual activity have no such substance and no such marks. This absence of self in phenomena (dharmanairātmya), which is the pure contemplation of suchness, is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
Therefore, the Tathāgata, relying on that dharma, speaks of the ultimate truth as being without intrinsic nature or characteristics.
“World-Honored One!
As it is with the Truth of Suffering, so it is with the remaining truths.”

In this way, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path—in short, all dharmas are likewise thus.
“World-Honored One!
I understand the meaning of the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One:

within the sphere of conceptual differentiation, based upon false discrimination, there arise the characteristics of conditioned activities; through the counteractive power of right awakening and samādhi, the counteractive right samādhi is produced.”
Having given rise to samādhi, one further maintains it, neither forgetting nor losing it, so that its cultivation increases.

The characteristics of dharmas and the superior characteristics described by names are merely marks of conceptual discrimination; therefore, the Tathāgata, relying on those characteristics of dharmas, declares that all dharmas have no intrinsic essence or characteristic.
World-Honored One!

That which is the basis for the realm of discrimination depends upon other-power; the mode of activity of causes and conditions is the characteristic of other-power. Therefore, the Tathāgata, relying on these dharmic characteristics, declares that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and characteristics, and he also declares that the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is without intrinsic nature and characteristics.
“World-Honored One!
I understand the meaning and characteristics of what the World-Honored One has taught:

that which is the basis for the conceptualization of names and the mode of activity of conceptualizing names—that very conceptualization lacks such characteristics; that which is without characteristics, that which is the essence of being without characteristics, the dharma of non-substantiality, and selflessness—the characteristic of the pure contemplation of suchness is the ultimate truth.”
Therefore, the World-Honored One has said that the absence of intrinsic nature and characteristics in all phenomena is the characteristic of the ultimate truth.
"World-Honored One!
It is like the viśvabhū medicinal herb, which is present within all other medicines and all foods."
World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is likewise: all dharmas are without essence or characteristics—dharmas are unarisen, dharmas are unceasing, dharmas are quiescent, and dharmas are by nature in nirvāṇa. Having expounded the sūtras of definitive meaning, he places them among all the sūtras of provisional meaning.
“World-Honored One!
It is like drawing on the ground with various colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—which all share the single characteristic of being drawn; one is thus able to discern those various painted forms.”
World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is likewise: all phenomena are without essence or characteristics—unborn, unceasing, quiescent, and by nature in nirvāṇa. This definitive teaching is placed among all non-definitive teachings to form a single flavor, for it is also able to discern the names of those non-definitive sūtras and so forth.
“World-Honored One!
Just as when mature ghee is added to all kinds of food and drink, it produces a superior flavor, so too is this Dharma taught by the Buddha:

based on the fact that all phenomena have no substantial nature—being unborn, unceasing, quiescent, and parinirvāṇa by their very nature—this sūtra of definitive meaning is placed among all the sūtras of non-definitive meaning, producing a superior sense of joy and exultation.”
“World-Honored One!
It is like space, which is equal in all places and encounters no obstruction regarding any of the various kinds of activities; it is able to accomplish them all.”
World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata is likewise; he declares that all dharmas have no essential nature or characteristics—that all dharmas are unarisen, all dharmas are unceasing, all dharmas are quiescent, and the self-nature of all dharmas is nirvāṇa. Having expounded the sūtras of definitive meaning, they are of one single flavor with all sūtras of provisional meaning, accomplishing the practice of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and those of the Mahāyāna, acting without obstruction.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Paramārthasiddhi, saying: “Excellent, Paramārthasiddhi!
He then spoke these words again:
“Excellent, excellent! You have accomplished the ultimate truth!
You truly are able to understand the intent behind the Dharma teachings spoken by all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.”
You have now skillfully explained this meaning through these similes, such as the *viśva* medicinal herb, drawing on the ground, placing ghee, and space.
You have established the ultimate truth!
"It is so, it is so, just as you have said.
It does not differ from what you have spoken; thus should it be upheld.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Paramārthasiddhi addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

When the Tathāgata first attained the state of an Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Sages near the city of Vārāṇasī—a place frequented by various birds and beasts—he turned for the sake of the śrāvaka practitioners engaged in cultivation the unprecedented Wheel of Dharma of the Four Noble Truths. No śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, human, māra, or Brahmā in the world is able to turn it; were anyone able to turn it, it would be impossible for that to accord with the Dharma.”
“World-Honored One!

This second turning of the wheel of Dharma explains the characteristics of the supreme Dharma that can enter the characteristics of the Dharma; it analyzes those various sūtras of provisional meaning for the sake of sentient beings dwelling in the Mahāyāna, teaching that all dharmas have no essential nature—namely, that all dharmas are unarisen, all dharmas are unceasing, all dharmas are quiescent, and all dharmas are by nature in nirvāṇa. Among rare things, this is most rare.”
“World-Honored One!

This is the third turning of the wheel of Dharma, spoken for the sake of all sentient beings who abide in the Mahāyāna, teaching that all phenomena are without essence or characteristics—unborn, unceasing, quiescent, and by nature in nirvāṇa. It skillfully explains the distinct characteristics of the Four Noble Truths; it is rare, most rare. No one can enter it, no one can oppose it, no one can dispute it; it is unsurpassed, peerless, the definitive sūtra, and a place free from contention.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Paramārthasiddhi addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears the Tathāgata teach that all dharmas are from the beginning without essence or characteristics—originally unarisen, originally unceasing, originally quiescent, and by nature originally in nirvāṇa—and with right faith writes them down, and having written them, receives and upholds them, makes offerings to them, gives them to others, recites them for oneself, chants them oneself, reads them oneself, practices them, and rejoices in them, how much merit will that son of good family or daughter of good family obtain?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Paramārthasiddhi, saying:
"Those sons of good family and daughters of good family shall accomplish an immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya mass of merit."
O you who have realized the ultimate truth!
His merits are beyond all analogy and cannot be fully described through comparison.
To state it briefly and concisely, I shall describe but a small portion.
“O you who have accomplished the ultimate truth!

It is like the dust upon a fingernail compared to the dust of the great earth: it does not equal even one hundredth part, nor one *kalā* part, nor one *upaniṣad* part; indeed, no calculation or analogy can reach even a fraction of it.”

“Siddhārtha! It is like the water in a cow’s footprint compared to the water of the great ocean: it does not equal one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor one *kalā* part, nor one *upaniṣad* part; indeed, even by calculation or analogy, it cannot be compared.”
“Pariniṣpanna-paramārtha! It is so;

I say that the merit obtained from faith in, and even the practice of, sūtras of provisional meaning—even compared to the merit obtained from generating faith in, practicing, upholding, reading, and reciting this sūtra of definitive meaning as it has been explained—the former merit of those sūtras of provisional meaning does not equal one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor ten thousandth part, nor one *kalā* part, nor one *upaniṣad* part; it is beyond all calculation and analogy.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Paramārthasiddhi addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Within this *Sūtra of the Liberation through Profound Secrecy*, what is the name of this Dharma-gate?”
"How should it be received and upheld?
The Buddha said:
"Accomplish the ultimate truth!"
"This Dharma-gate is named 'The Sūtra Explaining the Definitive Meaning of the Ultimate Truth'; you should receive and uphold it in this way.

When the Buddha spoke this Dharma-gate, six thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; three hundred thousand śrāvakas were freed from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; furthermore, five hundred thousand śrāvakas attained the liberation of the mind through the outflow-free state; and seventy-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
The Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra, Scroll Second;
The Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra, Scroll Third.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Nine: The Questions of the Noble Maitreya Bodhisattva (3–4).
At that time, the noble Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, relying on the characteristics of phenomena as encompassed by *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Bhagavān, upon what dharmas does a bodhisattva rely, and by means of what dharmas does he abide, so as to practice śamatha and vipaśyanā within the Mahāyāna?"
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: “Maitreya!
It is by relying on the exposition of the distinct characteristics of all phenomena and by being able to maintain the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
Maitreya! According to the four methods of contemplation that I have taught, bodhisattvas rely upon those four methods of contemplation to practice Mahāyāna śamatha and vipaśyanā.
What are the four? First, analytical contemplation; second, non-analytical contemplation; third, the differentiation of phenomena; and fourth, the accomplishment of what is to be done.
Maitreya Bodhisattva asked the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
How many kinds of śamatha contemplation are there?"
The Buddha said:
"Maitreya! There is only one kind of śamatha-vipaśyanā, namely, non-conceptual observation."
Maitreya Bodhisattva spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
How many kinds of vipaśyanā contemplation are there?"
The Buddha said:
“Maitreya! There is only one kind, namely, the contemplation of distinctions.”
Maitreya Bodhisattva spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
How many names are there for those who are directed toward the two contemplations?”
The Buddha said,
“Maitreya, there are two kinds:”
"The first is the differentiation of phenomena, and the second is the accomplishment of phenomena.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
"World-Honored One!"
How does a bodhisattva, relying on four kinds of dharmas, practice the contemplation of śamatha and vipaśyanā, and thereby skillfully know śamatha and vipaśyanā?
The Buddha said: “Maitreya!

As I have taught for the sake of the bodhisattvas, there are the various categories of dharma-characteristics, namely: sūtra, geya, vyākaraṇa, gāthā, udāna, nidāna, avadāna, itivṛttaka, jātaka, vaipulya, adbhutadharma, and upadeśa.”

Maitreya! Regarding such sūtras as these, all bodhisattvas should listen attentively and thoroughly, constantly recite them with their mouths, always understand them well with their minds, constantly observe them with wisdom, and realize them as they truly are through insight.
Maitreya! After those bodhisattvas have carefully contemplated those sūtras, they sit alone in a secluded place and observe; observing that mind, they constantly accord with it within.
Observing the mind in this way and maintaining the mind without interruption, that bodhisattva attains physical ease and mental ease.
Maitreya, this is what I call the bodhisattva’s practice of the dharma of śamatha.

“Once that bodhisattva has attained physical and mental bliss, he relies upon physical and mental bliss to contemplate the Dharma as it was taught. Just as he previously contemplated all phenomena, he observes the images within the realm of internal samādhi; thus he is able to have faith in all phenomena and become free from discursive thought.”

Maitreya! When bodhisattvas contemplate that mirror-image of samādhi in this manner, they can understand its meaning; through vitarka, vicāra, reflection, patience, aspiration, and the intention to see, their cognitive realization manifests before them.
Maitreya! This is what I call the bodhisattva’s practice of vipaśyanā. Maitreya!
"All bodhisattvas should thus skillfully understand vipaśyanā.
At that time, the noble Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Bhagavān! When a bodhisattva has not yet attained internal contemplation of the image, and has not yet attained physical ease or mental ease, what kind of contemplation does the Buddha call that?"
The Buddha said:
“Maitreya! It is not śamatha itself; it is that which accords with śamatha. Therefore, I say it is called ‘śamatha that accords with faith.’”
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!

When a bodhisattva has not yet attained physical ease or mental ease, but contemplates the sphere of the samādhi of the internal body and reflects upon those dharmas, thus observing the mind—what is the name of that contemplation which the Buddha teaches?”
The Buddha said:
"Maitreya! I say that this contemplation of theirs is not vipaśyanā; it is called 'vipaśyanā that accords with faith'."
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
Are the practice of śamatha and the practice of vipaśyanā one and the same, or are they different?”
The Buddha said:
"I say it is neither different nor not different, Maitreya."
For what reason do I say they are not different?
Because vipaśyanā observation is not separate from śamatha; therefore, they are not different, Maitreya!
"For what reason do I say they are different?
Because one observes the distinctions between the objects and their mental images through conceptualization, they are therefore different.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
Is the realm of the vipaśyanā-samādhi different from that mind, or not different from that mind?
The Buddha said:
“Maitreya! I say they are not different.
In what sense are they not different?
One contemplates those objective images as being solely mind.
Why is this? Because I teach that it is only by way of the designation "mind, mentation, and consciousness" that one attains the name [of such contemplation].
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
If that mental object and its image are not different from the mind, how can the mind itself observe the mind?”
The Buddha said, "Maitreya!
In that state, there is not a single dharma capable of observing another dharma; yet, such a direct perception arises from the mind."
Maitreya! It is like a pure, clear mirror: by depending on and taking objects as its cause, it can manifest those objects, yet it does not form the thought:
"I see these objects."
"By relying on those objective images, one perceives the objective images. Maitreya!
Just as that mind arises without being separate from the mind, yet one perceives objects apart from the mind, so too do the mirror-images of samādhi appear as perceived objects."
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
Are all the mental phenomena and objective realms such as form belonging to all sentient beings different from the mind, or are they not different from the mind?”
The Buddha said,
“Maitreya, it is not different from the mind.”

Yet ordinary beings, through their inverted cognition, fail to recognize that these are merely mental phenomena; because they do not know those various objective images as they truly are, they grasp at them with inversion and inverted dharmas.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva practice vipaśyanā exclusively?”
The Buddha said:
"Maitreya! If a bodhisattva continuously observes the characteristics of that mind in accordance with reality, such a bodhisattva practices vipaśyanā exclusively."
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva single-mindedly contemplate that dharma of śamatha?”
The Buddha said:
“Maitreya! If a bodhisattva continuously observes the characteristics of that mind in accordance with reality, in this way, the bodhisattva single-mindedly contemplates the dharma of śamatha.”
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
How do the two dharmas of a bodhisattva’s śamatha and vipaśyanā become integrated and practiced simultaneously?”
The Buddha said:
“Maitreya! If a bodhisattva contemplates the mind with single-mindedness, in this way, śamatha and vipaśyanā are practiced simultaneously.”
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
What is the characteristic of the mind?”
The Buddha said,
“Maitreya! That which is called the discernment of the mirror-image contemplation within the realm of samādhi is termed the characteristic of the mind.”
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
What is the immediate succession of the mind?”
The Buddha said:
"Maitreya! That which is called the śamatha contemplation of the mind that contemplates the image is termed 'uninterruptedness of mind'."
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
"World-Honored One!
What is this 'mind' of which you speak when you say 'one mind'?"
The Buddha said, “Maitreya!

That which is called observing the images within the realm of that samādhi and realizing them to be mind—having realized them to be mind, one cultivates the contemplation of True Suchness (tathatā). Maitreya!”
"This is called single-mindedness.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said,
"World-Honored One!"
"How many kinds of vipaśyanā practice are there?
The Buddha said, "Maitreya!"
Vipassanā is of three kinds. What are these three?
First, the sign; second, the practice; and third, the contemplation.
Maitreya! What is the vipaśyanā of signs?
It refers to observing only the images within the sphere of samādhi through discernment; this is called the vipaśyanā of signs.
Maitreya! What is the practice of vipaśyanā?
It is the wisdom that clearly perceives the specific characteristics of each and every phenomenon; this is called the practice of vipaśyanā.
Maitreya! What is the insight of vipaśyanā?
It is the wisdom that skillfully contemplates the specific characteristics of various phenomena within those respective phenomena, yet does not realize their cessation or liberation. Maitreya!
"This is called the skillful observation and practice of vipaśyanā.
Maitreya Bodhisattva spoke again:
"World-Honored One!"
“How many types of śamatha practice are there?
The Buddha said, “Maitreya!”
One should know that the latter three types are also to be understood in the same manner as the preceding method. Furthermore,
Maitreya, there are eight kinds of śamatha:

What is called the śamatha of the first dhyāna; likewise, the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, Maitreya,
there are four kinds of śamatha: namely,
śamatha of loving-kindness (maitrī), śamatha of compassion (karuṇā), śamatha of sympathetic joy (muditā), and śamatha of equanimity (upekṣā).
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
As the World-Honored One has taught, one relies upon śamatha and vipaśyanā, yet does not rely upon śamatha and vipaśyanā.”
World-Honored One!
What is the dharma that is dependent?
What is the dharma that is non-dependent?
The Buddha said: “Maitreya!
It is as you have heard the Dharma; it accords with the characteristics of the Dharma, Maitreya!”
This is called the *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* that rely upon the Dharma. Maitreya!

Apart from the Dharma as it has been heard, one contemplates and grasps the Dharma, relying on the instructions of others to contemplate the meaning of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*—namely, contemplating those various signs as blue, yellow, red, white, foul-smelling, or putrid; [contemplating] that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent and suffering, that all phenomena are selfless, and that all phenomena are tranquil and *nirvāṇa*. Such are the *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, Maitreya!
This is what should be understood as the śamatha and vipaśyanā that do not rely upon phenomena. Maitreya!
As for the śamatha and vipaśyanā that do rely upon phenomena, I have taught them in this way for those bodhisattvas of sharp faculties who follow the characteristics of phenomena.
“Maitreya! For those who do not rely on the Dharma but follow the teachings of others, I have made such a statement for the sake of those bodhisattvas of dull faculties.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
As the World-Honored One has taught, there is the method of discerning śamatha and vipaśyanā separately, and the method of not discerning śamatha and vipaśyanā separately.”
"Bhagavān! What is the method of śamatha and vipaśyanā through differentiated observation?
And what is the method of śamatha and vipaśyanā through non-differentiated observation?"
The Buddha said: “Maitreya!

If a bodhisattva contemplates each of the dharmas, such as the sūtras, just as they were heard and received, reflects upon all dharmas, and practices śamatha and vipaśyanā, this is called the method of differentiated contemplation of śamatha and vipaśyanā.”

“Maitreya! If a bodhisattva takes those very dharmas of the sūtras and so forth, and treats them as a single segment, a single portion, or a single collection, and thus contemplates all these dharmas as being in conformity with suchness, flowing toward suchness, inclining toward suchness, following that suchness, conforming to awakening, conforming to nirvāṇa, revolving in accordance with mind-consciousness, conforming to those dharmas, and inclining toward those dharmas—then, Maitreya, they are able to know, as they truly are, the characteristics of immeasurable, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) wholesome dharmas.”
"This is called the method of śamatha and vipaśyanā through non-discriminative contemplation.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
"World-Honored One!"
As the Blessed One has taught, there is the method of śamatha and vipaśyanā observed through subtle distinctions, and the method of śamatha and vipaśyanā observed through gross distinctions.
"Bhagavān! What is the method of śamatha and vipaśyanā that involves the contemplation of minor distinctions?
And what is the method of śamatha and vipaśyanā that involves the contemplation of major distinctions?"
“What, Maitreya, is this method of śamatha and vipaśyanā that involves the contemplation of the distinctions among immeasurable signs?
The Buddha said: “Maitreya!”
If a bodhisattva contemplates the sūtras individually, from one up to the upadeśas, as single units of thought, Maitreya,
this is called the method of śamatha and vipaśyanā through the contemplation of slight distinctions.
Maitreya! If a bodhisattva contemplates those very sūtras and so forth as a single, undifferentiated whole, Maitreya!
This is called the method of śamatha and vipaśyanā characterized by the contemplation of great marks and distinctions.

Maitreya! If a bodhisattva takes as a single object of contemplation the immeasurable dharmas, immeasurable names, immeasurable phrases, and immeasurable supreme wisdoms, eloquences, and analytical powers taught by the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, this is called the dharma of śamatha and vipaśyanā consisting of the contemplation of immeasurable distinctions.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva realize the distinct methods of śamatha and vipaśyanā?”
The Buddha said,
"Maitreya! There are five kinds of contemplation by which one contemplates those dharmas."
What are the five kinds? They are:
contemplating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, whereby one extinguishes all afflictions moment by moment;
and the body being detached from various signs, thereby attaining the bliss of the Dharma.
One knows, as they truly are, the ten directions as immeasurable and boundless;
one knows the portion of purity that corresponds to the accomplishment of the activities of the light of immeasurable dharmas;
and with non-conceptual marks manifesting before one, this serves as the cause for attaining the accomplishment of the Dharmakāya and realizing the progressively superior and most excellent states.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
In what place does one practice the differentiated contemplation of the dharmas of śamatha and vipaśyanā in accordance with them?”
"In what place is the method for attaining the distinct cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā realized?
The Buddha said, "Maitreya!"

Maitreya, it should be known that while a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva on the first Ground, the Joyful, realizes [this] only slightly in accordance with the truth, on the third Ground, the Luminous, they realize it well. Maitreya!
"Even a beginner bodhisattva practices this method of differentiated śamatha and vipaśyanā, because they train in contemplation without ceasing.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said,
"World-Honored One!"
What is the samādhi with vitarka and vicāra in śamatha and vipaśyanā?
What is the samādhi without vitarka but with vicāra?
And what is the samādhi without vitarka and without vicāra?
The Buddha said, “Maitreya! If a bodhisattva,

in accordance with what has been heard, takes up all dharmas, and regarding the coarse and subtle characteristics of applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra) within all dharmas, follows that which can give rise to the dharmas of śamatha and vipaśyanā— this is called the samādhi with applied thought and sustained thought.”

Maitreya! If a bodhisattva, regarding those characteristics of phenomena, does not clearly perceive their coarse and subtle aspects, yet practices in accordance with those phenomena and thereby attains the light of that dharma and a mind of right mindfulness, and accordingly observes them subtly through śamatha and vipaśyanā—Maitreya!
This is called the samādhi with no vitarka but with vicāra. Maitreya!
If a bodhisattva is free from all marks, spontaneously accords with the Dharma, and contemplates and observes śamatha and vipaśyanā, this is called the samādhi with neither vitarka nor vicāra.
"Furthermore, Maitreya! When one first practices śamatha and vipaśyanā, this is called the samādhi with vitarka and vicāra. Maitreya!"
If a bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena, this is called the samādhi of non-discursive thought with slight observation.
Maitreya! If a bodhisattva contemplates the samādhi of undifferentiated phenomena, this is called the samādhi of non-discursive thought and non-observation.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
What is the characteristic of śamatha?”
“What is the sign of grasping at śamatha?
What is the sign of equanimity toward śamatha?
The Buddha said:

“Maitreya! If, while the mind is agitated or in a state of doubt, a bodhisattva gives rise to a sense of alarm or fear, or desires to distance themselves from it, yet contemplates all phenomena without interruption—this is called the characteristic of śamatha.”
Maitreya! If a bodhisattva’s mind becomes sunken or suspects it is in a state of sinking, and by reflecting upon the Dharma gives rise to a heart of joy, this is called śamatha that grasps at signs.

Maitreya! If a bodhisattva, through the path of śamatha alone or the path of vipaśyanā alone, contemplates those two dharmas with both paths, such that afflictions do not defile the mind, and naturally reflects upon and naturally accords with the practice of those dharmas—this is called the characteristic of equanimity in śamatha.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
As the World-Honored One has taught, when a bodhisattva practices the dharmas of śamatha and vipaśyanā, they know phenomena as they truly are and know their meanings as they truly are.”
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva know the Dharma and know its meaning?
The Buddha said:
“Maitreya! If a bodhisattva knows five kinds of contemplative methods, this is called knowing phenomena as they truly are. What are these five?
First is name, second is phrase, third is syllable, fourth is distinction, and fifth is sameness.
Maitreya! What is a name?
Maitreya, it refers to observing the intrinsic characteristics within defiled and pure phenomena, and explaining their phenomenal characteristics;
this, Maitreya, is called "name. Maitreya!
What is a phrase (*pada*)?
It is the collection of various names for those very phenomena; taking the meaning of defiled and pure phenomena as the name, its function of providing a basis and support is called a phrase.
Maitreya! What is a syllable?
It is that which serves as the basis for those names and phrases; that which is named after a single dharma is called a syllable.
Maitreya! What is differentiation?
It refers to the distinct observation of each individual phenomenon; this is called differentiation.
Maitreya! What is this "sameness"?
It refers to the practice of non-discriminative contemplation; this is what is called sameness.
“Maitreya! If a bodhisattva contemplates in this manner, they are said to know phenomena as they truly are. Maitreya!”
What is the bodhisattva’s contemplation of meaning?
There are ten kinds of a bodhisattva’s contemplation of meaning. What are these ten?

First, practicing that which ought to be practiced; second, practicing until reaching the ultimate state; third, knowing the meaning of the grasper; fourth, knowing the meaning of the grasped; fifth, knowing the meaning of maintenance; sixth, knowing the meaning of enjoyment; seventh, knowing the meaning of inversion; eighth, knowing the meaning of non-inversion; ninth, knowing the meaning of defilement; and tenth, knowing the meaning of purity.

“Maitreya! If a bodhisattva practices all the various distinctions among the defiled and purified phenomena—namely, the fivefold enumeration of the aggregates (*skandha*), the sixfold enumeration of the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), and the sixfold enumeration of the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*)—and practices such distinctions, Maitreya!”
This is called the practice that a bodhisattva should perform.
"Maitreya! If a bodhisattva knows suchness as it truly is within both defiled and purified phenomena, Maitreya!"
This is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation reaching its ultimate point.
"Furthermore, Maitreya, there are seven kinds of *tathatā* (suchness)."
What are the seven? They are:
the suchness of the characteristics of beginningless conditioned formations;
and the suchness of characteristics, which refers to the emptiness of self and the emptiness of phenomena.
The suchness of consciousness-only is knowing that conditioned activities are nothing but mind;
the suchness of attachment is what I call the truth of suffering;
the suchness of wrong practice is what I call the truth of origination.
The suchness of purity is what I call the truth of cessation;
the suchness of correct practice is what I call the truth of the path. Maitreya!
The suchness of modes of activity, the suchness of attachment, and the suchness of wrong practice— these three types of suchness are equal and without distinction for all sentient beings, Maitreya!
The suchness of characteristics and the suchness of consciousness-only—these two suchnesses are equal and without distinction among all phenomena. Maitreya!
Pure suchness is equal and without distinction among śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Maitreya! One who practices suchness hears the sublime Dharma as it is; through the distinct contemplations of śamatha and vipaśyanā, one grasps the equality of prajñā, which is without distinction.

“Maitreya! When a bodhisattva knows the meaning of the grasper (*grāhaka*), it refers to the five kinds of entry-points (*praveśa-lakṣaṇa*), as well as mind (*citta*), mental faculty (*manas*), mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*); this is called knowing the meaning of the grasper.”
“Maitreya! That which is to be grasped as an object refers to the six external sense bases. Maitreya!”
The meaning of the grasper (*grāhaka*) is itself the meaning of the graspable (*grāhya*); this is called knowing the meaning of the grasper and the graspable. "Maitreya!

When a bodhisattva knows the meaning of abiding and maintaining, it refers to the world as the dwelling place of sentient beings; based on those dwelling places, sentient beings can be perceived, namely villages and fields."
A hundred clusters of lands, a thousand clusters of lands, and ten million clusters of lands are called the land reaching to the edge of the ocean;
a hundred thousand of those, or a hundred thousand Jambudvīpas,
or a hundred thousand and ten million of those, is called a small chiliocosm.
A hundred times that thousandfold world system, a thousand times that, and a hundred thousand times that is called a "two-thousandfold intermediate world system.
A hundred times, a thousand times, and a hundred thousand times that two-thousandfold intermediate world system is called a "trichiliocosm" (a three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system).
A hundred times that trichiliocosm, then again a thousand times, again a thousand times, then again a hundred thousand million times—that hundred thousand million times is called one *koṭi*.

One hundred times that billion, one thousand times that hundred, one billion times that thousand, one hundred billion times that billion, and again one hundred trillion times that—this is called one *asaṃkhyeya*.

One hundred billion times that thousand billion, one thousand billion times that hundred thousand billion, one hundred thousand billion *asaṃkhyeyas*, one hundred *asaṃkhyeyas* of *asaṃkhyeyas*, one thousand *asaṃkhyeyas* of hundred *asaṃkhyeyas*, one hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeyas* of hundred thousand million three-thousandfold great thousandfold world systems, one hundred thousand million *asaṃkhyeyas* of worlds, and as many as the number of atoms in one hundred thousand million [worlds]—in the worlds of the ten directions, Maitreya, there are immeasurable worlds.
This is called the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the meaning of sustaining.
"Maitreya! What is the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the meaning of livelihood?"
That is to say, it is because I have taught sentient beings the various means of livelihood and objects of enjoyment.
"Maitreya! What is the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the meaning of inversion?"

Maitreya! Regarding that very appropriation and enjoyment, there arise the inversion of the perception of permanence within the meaning of impermanence, the inversion of mind, and the inversion of view; the inversion of the perception of pleasure within suffering, the inversion of the perception of purity within the impure; and the inversion of the perception of self, the inversion of mind, and the inversion of view within non-self. Maitreya!
This is called the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the meaning of inversion. “Maitreya!
What is the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the meaning of non-inversion?”
“Maitreya! To be far removed from those four inversions is called a bodhisattva’s knowledge of the meaning of non-inversion. Maitreya!”
What is the meaning of the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the characteristics of defilement? Maitreya,
within the three realms there are three kinds of characteristics of defilement:
These are the defilement of afflictions, the defilement of karma, and the defilement of birth.
Maitreya, this is called the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the meaning of defilement.
“Maitreya! How does a bodhisattva know the meaning of purity? Maitreya!”
That is to say, Maitreya, by remaining far removed from those three kinds of defilements and practicing the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma),
this is called the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the meaning of purity. Maitreya!
"Maitreya, you should know that these ten kinds of meanings encompass all meanings;
this is called the bodhisattva’s characteristic of knowing meanings as they truly are.
Furthermore, Maitreya..."
If a bodhisattva knows five kinds of dharmas, that bodhisattva is said to be well-versed in the meaning.

What are these five? First, the knowable sphere; second, the knowable meaning; third, the knowledge of dharmas; fourth, attaining the realization of the fruit based on that knowledge; and fifth, receiving those dharmas as they truly are.
“Maitreya! What are the phenomena that can be known? Maitreya!”
"All objects—namely, the five aggregates, the internal sense bases, the external sense bases, and so forth—are called 'knowing objects. Maitreya!"
What is the meaning that can be known? Maitreya! One knows those dharmas as they truly are through immeasurable modes of contemplation—namely:

the conventional truth and the ultimate truth; dharmas of merit and dharmas of fault; dharmas of causes and conditions and dharmas of the three periods of time; dharmas of arising, abiding, and ceasing; dharmas such as illness; dharmas of suffering, its origin, and so forth; the dharma of suchness, the dharma of the limit of reality, and the dharma of the realm of phenomena; concise dharmas and extensive dharmas; dharmas of questions and answers explained with categorical distinctions and dharmas set aside for non-response; and secret dharmas and direct dharmas. Maitreya!
Such meanings as these should be understood.
Maitreya! What is the knowledge of phenomena?
“Maitreya! To be able to give rise to that knowledge of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path—Maitreya!
This is called knowing the Dharma.”
“Maitreya! What is the dharma that a bodhisattva realizes by relying on knowledge?

It is the cessation of the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion; the distancing oneself from the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion; and the attainment of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya—namely, what I call the merits of the śrāvakas, the Tathāgatas, the mundane, and the supramundane—all of which are realized and known as they truly are. Maitreya!”
This is called the bodhisattva’s reliance on the knowledge of the dharma for realizing the fruit. "Maitreya!
What is the bodhisattva’s correct reception of that dharma?"

Maitreya! That very Dharma which has been realized is known as liberation and experienced as liberation; furthermore, it is extensively expounded, demonstrated, and revealed for the sake of all sentient beings.
“Maitreya! You should know that these five dharmas encompass all meanings.
Furthermore, Maitreya!”
When a bodhisattva knows the four kinds of contemplation, it is called knowing the meaning as it truly is.
What are these four? They are:
knowing the meaning of the arising of the mind, knowing the meaning of experience, knowing the meaning of following the mind, and knowing the meaning of defilement and purity.
“Maitreya! You should know that when a bodhisattva ultimately attains four kinds of meaning, it is also called ‘comprehending all meanings.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva knows three kinds of phenomena as they truly are, this is called ‘knowing meanings as they truly are.’”
What are these three?
They are the meaning of the syllables, the meaning of the meanings, and the meaning of the elements (dhātu). Maitreya!
What is the meaning of "syllables" (*vyañjana*)?
Maitreya, you should know that it refers to the group of names (*nāmakāya*) and so forth;
this is the meaning of syllables.
Maitreya! What is the meaning of "the meaning of meanings"? Maitreya!
There are ten kinds of meaning. What are these ten?
They are, namely, the true mark;
The characteristic of knowing;
the characteristic of distancing oneself; the characteristic of realization.
The characteristics of practice are the characteristics of reality and so forth;
the characteristics of various distinctions;
and the characteristics of the relationship between the basis and that which is based upon it, which are the characteristics of obstacles to the knowledge of those [realities] and so forth.
Conforming to the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), not knowing the characteristics of faults, and knowing the characteristics of benefit—
Maitreya, these are called the bodhisattva’s characteristics for knowing the meaning of meanings.
“Maitreya! What is the characteristic of the meaning of the elements (dhātu) known by a bodhisattva? Maitreya!”
The characteristics of the meaning of "realms" (dhātu) are fivefold:
namely, the world-realm, the realm of sentient beings, the dharma-realm, the realm of those to be converted, and the realm of the skillful means for conversion. Maitreya!
"It should be understood that these five kinds of elements encompass all meanings.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Regarding what are called the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), calm abiding (*śamatha*), and insight (*vipaśyanā*)—the meaning of these three types of practice:
how do these three kinds of wisdom differ?
The Buddha said, “Maitreya!

One who practices through the wisdom of hearing relies upon names; as it is heard, it does not accord with their intent. This is not liberation manifest before one, nor is it liberation that accords with reality, Maitreya!”
This is called the meaning of the practice of the wisdom derived from hearing.
Maitreya! As for the meaning of the practice of the wisdom derived from reflection, Maitreya!

Maitreya, wisdom born of reflection also relies on names and words; it is merely as one has heard them and does not accord with the mind in such a way that liberation is manifest. Rather, it gradually accords with liberation, yet liberation is not directly realized. Maitreya!
This is called the meaning of the practice of wisdom through reflection.
Maitreya! As for the meaning of the practice of wisdom through cultivation, Maitreya!

Maitreya! A bodhisattva relies on names yet does not rely on names; relies on what has been heard yet does not rely on what has been heard; follows the mind and follows the knowable dharmas through wisdom; and as images appear before them within the sphere of samādhi, they increasingly conform to liberation and increase their liberation.
This is called the meaning of the practice of wisdom through cultivation.
Maitreya! This is called the meaning of the distinct characteristics of the three types of wisdom.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva practices śamatha and vipaśyanā, what constitutes wisdom?”
"What is meant by 'viewing'?
The Buddha said, "Maitreya!"
I shall now describe the characteristics of that immeasurable wisdom and vision.
To speak briefly: within the characteristics of diverse phenomena, the wisdom of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is what is termed "wisdom."
“Maitreya! To contemplate all dharmas as having no marks of differentiation—this is called ‘seeing.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva practices śamatha and vipaśyanā, with what kind of mind does he contemplate the characteristics of what phenomena?
The Buddha said:

“Maitreya! When contemplating the mind as suchness (tathatā), one practices the characteristics of phenomena (dharma-lakṣaṇa) and the characteristics of meaning (artha-lakṣaṇa); yet one does not perceive names, nor does one perceive the essential characteristics of names, nor does one perceive the causal characteristics of those names.”

In this manner, one should understand all meanings of phrases and syllables; even until one does not perceive the intrinsic characteristics of the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), yet perceives their causal characteristics, one practices *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
"This is what should be understood as the meaning of practicing śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
"World-Honored One!"
“Does a bodhisattva who practices the characteristics of the meaning of suchness also practice those characteristics?
The Buddha said, “Maitreya!”
The characteristics of true thusness (tathatā) cannot be seen as having any marks.
If there are no marks, how can one practice? Maitreya!

When a bodhisattva practices the characteristic of suchness, they subdue all phenomena and all characteristics of meaning; yet those phenomena cannot subdue the characteristic of the meaning of suchness.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!

The World-Honored One has often taught that when a vessel is impure, a mirror is impure, or water and the like are turbid, one cannot see the features of a face; however, when vessels and the like are pure, one can see the features of a face.”
"So it is, World-Honored One!
Those who do not practice with a mind of suchness cannot perceive the characteristics of all phenomena; those who do practice, World-Honored One, can perceive them."
“By means of what kind of mind does one contemplate which suchness when practicing contemplation?
Please explain this meaning. The Buddha said, “Maitreya!”
I have explained this meaning based on three kinds of contemplation.
What are these three?
They are the wisdom of hearing, the wisdom of reflection, and the wisdom of cultivation; it is through these three types of contemplative mind that one can realize suchness.
“Maitreya! It is based on this meaning that I have spoken.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva thus understands the meaning of all dharmas and practices the characteristics of all dharmas, how many dharma-characteristics are difficult to practice?
By means of which dharmas and which contemplations does one contemplate those that are difficult to practice?”
The Buddha said: “Maitreya!
There are ten kinds of characteristics of difficult practice; one contemplates those characteristics of difficult practice by means of the eighteen kinds of emptiness.”
What are these ten? Maitreya! They are:

observing the characteristics of the meaning of phenomena (*dharma-artha-lakṣaṇa*) and the characteristics of various names; relying on the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma-śūnyatā*), one severs those characteristics that are difficult to practice.

“Maitreya! One should experience the characteristics of reality as they truly are—namely, the characteristic of arising, the characteristic of cessation, the characteristic of abiding, the characteristic of change, and the characteristic of associated formations—by means of the emptiness of characteristics and the emptiness of beginninglessness, thereby severing those characteristics that are difficult to practice.”

“Maitreya! One who grasps at the characteristics of the object and the subject—namely, those based on the characteristic of a body and those based on the characteristic of a self—should sever those characteristics that are difficult to practice by relying on internal emptiness and the emptiness of non-perception.”

“Maitreya! The grasping at the characteristics of what is to be grasped—that is, the characteristics of the means of subsistence—is severed by relying on external emptiness; this severs those characteristics that are difficult to practice. Maitreya!”

Regarding the objects of appropriation—the male and female forms and various means of livelihood, namely the marks of internal and external purity—one severs those marks that are difficult to practice by relying on internal and external emptiness and the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
“Maitreya! The meaning of upholding [the Dharma] has immeasurable characteristics; by relying on great emptiness, one severs those characteristics that are difficult to practice. Maitreya!”

One takes up the characteristics of practicing the formless, the characteristics of internal tranquility and liberation, and relying on conditioned emptiness, one abandons those characteristics that are difficult to practice. "Maitreya!

Regarding the meaning of grasping the characteristics of *tathatā*—namely, the emptiness of self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), which are the ultimate characteristics of mind alone—one relies upon fundamental emptiness, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, and the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) to sever those characteristics that are difficult to practice.

“Maitreya! By grasping the characteristic of the unconditioned true thusness—which is in meaning free from all characteristics and devoid of differentiated characteristics—and by relying on the emptiness of the unconditioned and the non-differentiated emptiness, one severs those characteristics that are difficult to practice.”

“Maitreya! One takes that unconditioned emptiness (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*) and non-differentiated emptiness (*anantara-śūnyatā*) in order to sever the marks of those two types of emptiness; by means of the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), which serves as the antidote to unconditioned emptiness and non-differentiated emptiness, one severs those two forms of emptiness.”
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One,
when a bodhisattva practices these ten kinds of signs in this way, from what kind of bonds and signs does he attain liberation?”
The Buddha said: “Maitreya!

When one practices the realm of samādhi and attains liberation from the afflictions of attachment and bondage within the perception of forms and images, one contemplates those reflected images without grasping at the characteristics of the objects; this is called severing the characteristics that are difficult to practice.”

Maitreya, you should know that, speaking in terms of distinctions, these various forms of emptiness correspond to ten types of characteristics; it is not the case that each individual emptiness is unable to counteract and sever those ten types of characteristics.

Maitreya! For example, ignorance cannot directly produce birth, nor even the afflictions such as old age and death; however, it is said that "ignorance conditions volitional formations" based on the fundamental statement, speaking thus by way of proximate causes and conditions.
"Maitreya! This meaning should be understood in this way.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
What is the mark of concise emptiness?
A bodhisattva knows that mark of concise emptiness without losing any of the marks of emptiness, and remains free from all conceit regarding the mark of emptiness.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying:
“Excellent, Maitreya! Excellent, excellent!”
Maitreya! You are now able to ask the Buddha about this meaning. Maitreya!
It is excellent that you have asked this question in order not to lose the characteristic of emptiness for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
Why is this? Maitreya!
If a bodhisattva does not understand the characteristic of emptiness, they will lose all the characteristics of the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Maitreya, listen attentively now; I shall explain for you the meaning of emptiness in its abbreviated form.

Maitreya! Within the characteristics of other-power, the characteristics of the ultimate truth, and all phenomena, there are no characteristics of defilement or purity. That characteristic of false conceptualization is eternally free from those characteristics; one does not perceive any characteristic—this is called the brief explanation of emptiness within the Mahāyāna.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
"World-Honored One!
How many kinds of samādhis are subsumed within śamatha and vipaśyanā?"
The Buddha said, “Maitreya!
When I speak of the various samādhis— namely, the samādhis of śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas— you should know that they encompass all those samādhis.”
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
What kind of causes for dharmas can śamatha and vipaśyanā accomplish?”
The Buddha said, “Maitreya!
It can accomplish the cause for pure precepts, and it can accomplish the causes for the vision of wisdom derived from hearing and wisdom derived from reflection.”
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
What kind of fruit is produced by those causes of pure morality and the wisdoms of hearing and reflection?”
The Buddha said,
“Maitreya! It can accomplish the fruit of mental purity and the fruit of wisdom purity.”
Furthermore, Maitreya!
You should know that the fruits of śamatha and vipaśyanā of all śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas are able to accomplish all mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One,
what functions do śamatha and vipaśyanā perform?”
The Buddha said:
"Maitreya! One should remain far removed from two kinds of bonds."
What are these two?
They are the distancing from the bonds of signs and the distancing from the bonds of afflictions. Maitreya!
"This is called the activity of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
"World-Honored One!"
The Buddha taught five kinds of hindrances.
How many of these hinder śamatha? How many hinder vipaśyanā?
"How many types of inclinations are there toward the two obstacles? The Buddha said, "Maitreya!"
Attachment to the body and to the necessities of life— these two are hindrances to *śamatha*. Maitreya,
not rejoicing upon hearing all the wholesome dharmas taught by the Noble Ones is a hindrance to *vipaśyanā*.
Maitreya! One should know that these two—delighting in noisy and bustling places, and being content with meager attainment—are obstacles to śamatha and vipaśyanā. Maitreya!
"In places of noisy commotion, one cannot give rise to the practice of the Dharma; being satisfied with a mere trifle, one cannot ultimately attain the state of finality.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said, "World-Honored One!"
The Tathāgata has taught five kinds of hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
How many are obstacles to *śamatha*,
and how many are obstacles to *vipaśyanā*?
“How many are directed toward the two obstacles?
The Buddha said, “Maitreya!”
“Excitement and remorse are obstacles to śamatha; sleep and doubt are obstacles to vipaśyanā; and the two types, desire and anger, are obstacles to both.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said, “World-Honored One!”
“What, Maitreya, is the path of perfectly pure śamatha?
The Buddha said: “Maitreya!”
“Skillfully subduing sleep—this is called being well able to purify the path of śamatha.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!”
"What is the path of perfectly pure vipaśyanā?
The Buddha said, "Maitreya!"
"If one can skillfully sever the two hindrances of restlessness and regret, this is called being well able to purify the path of vipaśyanā.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
"World-Honored One!"
"Bodhisattvas practicing the path of śamatha and vipaśyanā— how many kinds of factors are there that cause one to know the mind is distracted and thus not called 'concordant'?
The Buddha said, "Maitreya!"
A bodhisattva knows five kinds of distraction, namely:
distraction of right mindfulness, external mental distraction, internal mental distraction, distraction of signs, and distraction of afflictions.
“Maitreya! If a bodhisattva abandons the signs associated with right mindfulness of the Mahāyāna and follows after the signs of mindfulness associated with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, Maitreya!”
This is called the bodhisattva’s distraction of right mindfulness. "Maitreya!

If a bodhisattva is attached to the five external sensual desires, delights in places of clamor and bustle, is attached to various discursive thoughts and investigations, and follows after thoughts that accord with the signs of the afflictions, this is called external mental distraction."
“Maitreya! If a bodhisattva is hindered by sleep, or if their mind is attached to a samādhi or other samādhis and samāpattis, or if they are defiled by that which causes defilement—Maitreya!”
This is called internal mental distraction. "Maitreya!
If a bodhisattva contemplates based on external signs or the signs of the objective realm of internal-body samādhi, this is called mental distraction."
“Maitreya! If a bodhisattva, relying on mental reflection upon causes and conditions, gives rise to discursive thought and afflictions—thinking ‘such a mind is I’—Maitreya!”
"This is called the distraction of the mind by afflictions.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said,
"World-Honored One!"
“Śamatha and vipaśyanā— from the first bodhisattva stage up to the stage of the Tathāgata— what faults do they counteract?
The Buddha said, “Maitreya!”
Śamatha and vipaśyanā counteract the afflictions arising from karma that leads to the evil realms within the first bhūmi;
they counteract subtle transgressions within the second bhūmi;
and they counteract the fault of desiring to acquire wholesome dharmas within the third bhūmi.
In the fourth stage, one remedies the fault of the mind regarding attachment to samādhi;
in the fifth stage, one remedies the fault of the world and nirvāṇa appearing either exclusively or non-exclusively;
and in the sixth stage, one remedies the fault of the activity of various signs.
In the seventh stage, one remedies the fault of subtle conceptual activity;
in the eighth stage, one remedies the faults of signless activity and spontaneous activity;
in the ninth stage, one remedies the fault of not attaining mastery in the teaching of the Dharma in all its aspects.
In the tenth stage, one counteracts the fault of not having attained the fulfillment of the dharmakāya;
Maitreya, in the eleventh stage, one counteracts the subtle, extremely subtle, and most subtle cognitive obscurations.
Maitreya! Once the bodhisattva has severed all those obstacles, he attains the state of unobstructed omniscience, accomplishes the dharmas he seeks, and realizes the pure dharmakāya.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
"World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva practice śamatha and vipaśyanā to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
The Buddha said: “Maitreya!

When a bodhisattva practices śamatha and vipaśyanā, they take the seven kinds of suchness as their basis. Just as they have heard and reflected upon the Dharma, they enter the concentrated mind and then recollect that Dharma; through the wisdom of hearing and reflection, they skillfully contemplate the distinctions within the internal mind and observe that suchness.”
When a bodhisattva contemplates that dharma of suchness, they abandon even the subtle mind of practice, let alone coarse dharmas.
"Maitreya! What are the characteristics of the subtle mind of practice?"

That which is called the arising of mind-consciousness, the experiencing of mind-consciousness, and the consciousness of defilement and purity; that which pertains to the internal, the external, and both; that which acts for the benefit of all sentient beings; the wisdom of *tathatā*—namely, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; the conditioned and the unconditioned; the permanent and the impermanent; the fact that the self-nature of suffering and its origin is not different [from emptiness]; the characteristics of karma and the conditioned; and the characteristics of the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena—one practices the mind of equanimity toward such dharmas as these.

Maitreya! When a bodhisattva thus arouses the mind and practices, and practices extensively in this way, moment by moment they become free from all hindrances and attain a pure mind. Having attained a pure mind, they enter the seven kinds of suchness; it should be known that they internally realize those seven kinds of awakening. Maitreya!
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s excellent attainment of the path of vision.

Once the bodhisattva has attained that wisdom of the path of vision, they are termed a bodhisattva of the fixed assembly; born into the family of the Buddhas, they enjoy the first bhūmi with benefit and joy.
This bodhisattva has previously practiced the paths of śamatha and vipaśyanā, and now for the first time attains the contemplation that brings the matter to its ultimate conclusion;
furthermore, as this bodhisattva practices within the progressively higher stages, by maintaining mindfulness of those two types of contemplation, they become detached from all subtle marks.
“Maitreya! It is like a person skillfully using a fine wedge to extract a coarse wedge. Maitreya!”
The practice of a bodhisattva is also like this: they observe the characteristics of the internal mind and depart from all those defiled objective aspects;
having departed from those defiled objective aspects, they depart from grasping at the characteristics of all wholesome dharmas;
and having departed from grasping at the characteristics of all wholesome dharmas, they depart from all characteristics.

In this successive manner, by recollecting similar dharmas within each progressively higher stage, the inner mind becomes pure until one realizes *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, thereby attaining the fulfillment of the contemplative practices of the cultivation to be performed.
"Maitreya! By practicing in this way, a bodhisattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
— *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, Scroll Three.
The Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra, Scroll Four,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Part Two of the Chapter on the Questions of Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
"World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, practicing the bodhisattva path, presently attain the various supreme and wondrous fruits of a bodhisattva?"
The Buddha said, “Maitreya!
If a bodhisattva can truly know these six kinds of dharmas, such a person will be able to attain the sublime fruit of a bodhisattva.”
What are the six kinds? They are:

skillfully knowing the arising of the mind, skillfully knowing the abiding of the mind, skillfully knowing the emergence of the mind, skillfully knowing the arrival of dharmas, skillfully knowing the increase of wholesome dharmas, and skillfully knowing expedient means.
“Maitreya! How does a bodhisattva skillfully know the arising of the mind? Maitreya!”
If a bodhisattva knows that sixteen kinds of mind arise, namely:
the non-awakening, non-knowing, and unmoving consciousness of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), which is like the *ādāna-vijñāna*;

the consciousness that perceives various marks, which is like simultaneously grasping objective spheres such as form; and the non-conceptual mental consciousness that cognizes internal and external forms, entering immeasurable samādhis in a single thought-moment, seeing immeasurable Buddha-lands, and seeing immeasurable Buddhas.
Maitreya! Consciousness associated with the contemplation of minor signs is, for example, like consciousness associated with the signs of the desire realm; Maitreya!
Consciousness associated with the contemplation of great signs is, for example, like consciousness associated with the signs of the form realm; Maitreya,
consciousness associated with the contemplation of immeasurable signs is, for example, like consciousness associated with all signs of space and all consciousnesses.
Maitreya! Consciousness associated with subtle characteristics is, for example, like consciousness associated with minor characteristics; Maitreya!
Consciousness associated with the contemplation of pervasive characteristics is, for example, like consciousness associated with the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; Maitreya,
consciousness associated with the contemplation of extremely subtle characteristics is, for example, like consciousness associated with supramundane characteristics.
Maitreya! Consciousness associated with the contemplation of the characteristic of suffering is, for example, like consciousness in the evil realms; Maitreya!
Consciousness associated with the contemplation of the characteristic of diversity and the characteristic of sensation is, for example, like consciousness in the desire realm; Maitreya,
consciousness associated with the contemplation of the characteristic of joy is, for example, like consciousness in the first and second dhyānas.
Maitreya! Consciousness associated with the contemplation of the aspect of pleasure is, for example, like the consciousness of the third dhyāna; Maitreya!

Consciousness associated with the contemplation of the sign of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure is, for example, like the consciousness of the fourth dhyāna up to that of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
Maitreya, consciousness associated with the contemplation of the sign of defilement is, for example, like consciousness that accords with and follows defiled afflictions.

Maitreya! Consciousness associated with the contemplation of the characteristics of wholesome dharmas is, for example, like consciousness associated with the cultivation of faith and so forth; Maitreya!
Consciousness associated with the contemplation of the indeterminate characteristic is, for example, like consciousness that is detached from those two dharmas.
Maitreya, this is called a bodhisattva’s knowledge of the arising of all dharmas.
“Maitreya! How does a bodhisattva know the abiding of all phenomena as they truly are? Maitreya!”
If a bodhisattva is able to know, according to reality, that these are merely the substance of consciousness, this is called a bodhisattva’s knowledge of the abiding of all phenomena. "Maitreya,
how does a bodhisattva skillfully know the arising of all phenomena?"
Maitreya! If a bodhisattva can truly know the two kinds of signs that bind one with afflictions, and having known them, reflects thus:
"I should abandon these phenomena."
“Maitreya! A bodhisattva who is thus is said to be well-versed in the arising of all phenomena. Maitreya!”
"How does a bodhisattva skillfully know the coming of dharmas? Maitreya!

If a bodhisattva skillfully knows that those afflictions are countered and the mind increases, and having known the increase of all dharmas, this is called a bodhisattva skillfully knowing the increase of my dharma."
“Maitreya! How does a bodhisattva skillfully know the inferiority of all phenomena? Maitreya!”
If a bodhisattva knows those remedial dharmas—that is, the afflictions and defiled characteristics that cause the mind to diminish—and well understands the diminution of all dharmas, Maitreya!
This is called a bodhisattva’s skillful knowledge of the diminution of all dharmas.
“Maitreya! How does a bodhisattva skillfully know expedient means? Maitreya!”
If a bodhisattva contemplates liberation, the spheres of mastery, and the spheres of totality, Maitreya!
This is called a bodhisattva’s skillful knowledge of expedient means.
"Maitreya! [he said].
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who skillfully know how to practice the bodhisattva path in this way are able to attain the most supreme and wondrous fruit of a bodhisattva.

Maitreya! All bodhisattvas of the past were likewise; all bodhisattvas of the future will be likewise; and all bodhisattvas of the present are likewise—by practicing the bodhisattva path, they attain the wondrous fruit of a bodhisattva.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata has often taught that within the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder, all sensations are extinguished without exception.”
“World-Honored One!
What is that characteristic of sensation (vedanā-lakṣaṇa) such that you say all characteristics of sensation are extinguished?
The Buddha said:

“Maitreya! Briefly stated, there are two kinds of cessation of sensation: namely, the cessation of the perception of the body and sensation, and the cessation of the perception of sensation toward the objective realm that is the fruit thereof. Maitreya!”
Regarding the cessation of the characteristics of bodily sensation, one should know that there are four kinds of sensation.
What are these four? They are:

the characteristic of sensation based on form, the characteristic of sensation based on the non-material, the characteristic of sensation that has achieved its fruit, and the characteristic of sensation that has not achieved its fruit.
“Maitreya! That which is the characteristic of experiencing the fruition of accomplishment refers to the characteristic of experiencing in the present;
that which is the characteristic of not accomplishing the fruition of experience refers to the cause-experience in future lives.”
“The characteristics of the experience of the realm of its retribution also consist of four kinds, namely:
the characteristic of sustaining experience, the characteristic of livelihood experience, the characteristic of enjoyment experience, and the characteristic of confronting experience.”

“Maitreya! Within the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder, the fruit of the characteristic of feeling is not yet fully accomplished; rather, there is the feeling resulting from contact associated with clear knowledge. Therefore, because all characteristics of feeling have not yet been extinguished, it is said that there remain characteristics of feeling based upon that.”

Maitreya! When the characteristics of the fruit and the characteristics of sensation are accomplished in all their aspects, those two characteristics of sensation cease, and there remains only the characteristic of sensation born of contact with clarity (*vimala-sparśa*).

Within the realm of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*), even that sensation ceases, because within nirvana without remainder there is no further characteristic of contact with clarity.
"Therefore, I say that within *nirvāṇa* without remainder, all characteristics of sensation (*vedanā*) are extinguished.
