At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Maitreya! Because you practice according to reality, you ask about the characteristics of the bodhisattva’s conduct that is fulfilled and pure. Maitreya!
"You have well studied and fully mastered the Dharma of practice according to reality; therefore, you ask me about the Dharma of practice according to reality.
Maitreya! You should know that I have already well explained the Dharma of the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of pure practice. Maitreya!"
The Buddhas of the past spoke thus; the Buddhas of the future will speak thus; the Buddhas of the present speak thus. All sons of good family of the past, future, and present have also asked thus.
"Therefore, all good sons and good daughters should practice the bodhisattva path with a sincere mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"In this practice of the Dharma, if a person is not heedless,"
The wise person who practices right reflection can attain the unsurpassed path.
If a person grasps at the marks of phenomena and seeks the essence of those phenomena, they depart from the practice of suchness; it is as incompatible as space and the earth.
Perceiving the nature of sentient beings, one is courageous in benefiting them;
attaining the mark of non-attachment, one gains all supramundane virtues.
Seeking to preach the Dharma for their sake, that person shall in turn attain the Dharma.
Having obtained that priceless treasure, he wanders through the world as a mendicant.
Liberated from all conceptual proliferation, his diligent practice is firm;
for the benefit of sentient beings, he cultivates this true practice.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
within this *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, by what name should this Dharma-gate be known?"
"How should it be upheld?
The Buddha said, "Maitreya!"
"This dharma-gate is named 'The Sūtra of Definitive Meaning on Practice According to Reality'; you should uphold it.

When this Sūtra of Definitive Meaning on Practice According to Reality was spoken, six thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; three thousand śrāvakas became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye; one hundred and five thousand śrāvakas were freed from all outflows, attaining liberation of mind; and seventy-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the accomplishment of the Mahāyāna contemplation of practice according to reality.

Chapter Ten: The Inquiry of the Holy Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (4–5). Part One of Chapter Ten: The Inquiry of the Holy Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. At that time, the holy Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
The World-Honored One has expounded for the bodhisattvas the distinctions of the ten stages, namely:

the Stage of Joy, the Stage of Purity, the Stage of Radiance, the Stage of Blazing, the Stage Difficult to Conquer, the Stage of Presence, the Stage of Far-Going, the Immovable Stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence, the Stage of the Dharma Cloud, and the eleventh, the Buddha Stage.
"Bhagavān! How many kinds of purity are there?
Into how many divisions are these stages subsumed?"
The Buddha said:
“Avalokiteśvara! You should know that these stages are comprised of four kinds of purity and eleven divisions.”

Avalokiteśvara! Superior purity of conduct encompasses the first stage; superior purity of ethical discipline encompasses the second stage; superior purity of mind encompasses the third stage; superior purity of wisdom encompasses the fourth stage, and so on up to the most supreme and wondrous stages from the fourth stage through to the Buddha-stage.
"O Avalokiteśvara! These are known as the four kinds of purity that encompass all the stages (bhūmi);
this should be understood. O Avalokiteśvara!"
What is the meaning of the eleven stages as they are subsumed? Avalokiteśvara!

From the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Practice through Faith (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), one practices ten kinds of faith and is able to skillfully contemplate the Bodhisattva Vehicle. Having transcended that stage of practice through faith, one enters the stage of certainty (*niyāma*) and fulfills those stages.
Avalokiteśvara! Although those bodhisattvas have fulfilled that portion, they are still unable to practice in accordance with reality regarding subtle conduct.

Those bodhisattvas who have not yet fulfilled that portion practice with diligent seeking in order to fulfill it; and even though they have fulfilled that portion, they are still unable to truly fulfill the worldly samādhis and samāpattis, nor have they fulfilled the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining.

Those bodhisattvas have not yet fulfilled those factors; in order to fulfill them, they practice with diligence and seek to attain fulfillment of those factors. Although they have fulfilled those factors—which are like the factors of enlightenment—they are still unable to practice them according to reality, as their minds cannot relinquish attachment to samādhi and the Dharma.

Those bodhisattvas have not yet fulfilled those factors; in order to fulfill them, they practice with diligence and seek to attain fulfillment of those factors. Although they have fulfilled those factors, they are still unable to observe all the truths (satya) as they truly are, nor can they relinquish the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment subsumed under skillful means (upāya), such that both the mundane and nirvāṇa appear before them exclusively, or do not appear at all.

Those bodhisattvas have not yet fulfilled that portion; in order to fulfill it, they practice with diligence and seek to attain its fulfillment. Although they may fulfill that portion, they are still unable to know the birth and death of all worlds as they truly are, nor can they extensively cultivate the practice of direct perception and signless right mindfulness.

Those bodhisattvas have not yet fulfilled that portion; in order to fulfill it, they practice with diligence and seek to attain its fulfillment. Although they may fulfill that portion, they are still unable to know, as it truly is, the uninterrupted and continuous signless right mindfulness, nor can they extensively cultivate it.

Those bodhisattvas have not yet fulfilled that portion; in order to fulfill it, they practice with diligence and seek to attain its fulfillment. Although they have fulfilled that portion, they are still unable to abandon the practice of signlessness (animitta) and act spontaneously, nor do they attain mastery within the practice of signlessness.

Those bodhisattvas have not yet fulfilled that portion; in order to fulfill it, they practice with diligence and seek to attain its fulfillment. Although they have fulfilled that portion, they are still unable to teach all dharmas without obstruction regarding those various names and signs, nor can they attain mastery in the teaching of the Dharma.

Those bodhisattvas have not yet fulfilled that portion; in order to fulfill it, they practice with diligence and seek to attain its fulfillment. Although they have fulfilled that portion, they are unable to attain the fulfillment of the dharma-body (dharmakāya), nor can they attain the enjoyment-body (sambhogakāya).

Those bodhisattvas do not fulfill that portion; in order to fulfill it, they practice with diligence and seek until they fulfill that portion. Although they have fulfilled that portion, they are still unable to attain the perfection of wisdom that is unobstructed and unhindered regarding the marks of all objective spheres.

Those bodhisattvas do not fulfill that portion; in order to fulfill it, they practice with diligence and seek until they fulfill that portion. Having fulfilled that portion, it is called the fulfillment of all factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). Having attained the fulfillment of enlightenment, the bodhisattva is named a Buddha.
"Ārya Avalokiteśvara!
You should know that the various stages are subsumed within these eleven kinds of divisions.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason does the World-Honored One say that the first is named the Ground of Joy, and so on, up to the Buddha-ground, which is called the Buddha-ground?
The Buddha said:

“Āvalokiteśvara! When a bodhisattva first leaves birth and death and attains the great supramundane benefit—pure, supreme, and wondrous—they experience joy and exultation; therefore, the first stage is called the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi).
Because they have distanced themselves from all subtle obstacles of violating the precepts, the second is called the Stage of Purity (Vimalā-bhūmi).”

Because it relies on the radiance of immeasurable wisdom to illuminate all samādhis and the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining, thereby attaining mastery and being able to produce light, the third stage is named the Ground of Radiance (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*).

Because the flames of the fire of wisdom blaze intensely, burning away the afflictions and habitual tendencies that obstruct the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), the fourth is named the Ground of Blazing Fire (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).

Because one practices those very factors of enlightenment through skillful means, attaining victory where it was difficult to conquer, the fifth is named the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*).

By means of right mindfulness, one contemplates all conditioned phenomena and realizes before one’s eyes that all dharmas are signless; therefore, the sixth stage is named the Ground of Presence (*Abhimukhī*).

Because of uninterrupted and unceasing right mindfulness that is signless, one enters far into practice and draws near to the ground of purity; therefore, the seventh stage is named the Ground of Far-Going (*Dūraṃgamā*).
Because there are no signs and one practices spontaneously, such that signs cannot cause movement, the eighth stage is named the Ground of Immovability (*Acalā*).

Because one teaches all dharmas with unimpeded mastery of all modes of knowledge and attains vast wisdom that cannot be overcome by others, the ninth stage is named the Stage of Excellent Wisdom (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*).

Because the bodies of sentient beings, burdened by afflictions and defects, are like space, while the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is like a great cloud that covers the realm of sentient beings to manifest and preach the Dharma, the tenth stage is named the Stage of the Dharma Cloud (*Dharmameghā-bhūmi*).

Because one is free from all subtle habitual tendencies of ignorance and free from all habitual tendencies of cognitive obstructions regarding objective spheres, being without hindrance or obstruction and attaining sovereignty over all dharmas, the eleventh stage is named the Buddha-stage (*Buddha-bhūmi*).
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!”
“How many kinds of ignorance are there in these stages?
And how many kinds of obstacles do they counteract? The Buddha said:
“Āvalokiteśvara! There are twenty-two kinds of ignorance and eleven kinds of hindrances. Āvalokiteśvara!”

In the first stage (*bhūmi*), there is the ignorance that clings to the self of persons and the self of phenomena, and the ignorance regarding the defiled characteristics of the afflictions of the evil realms; because one is deluded and submerged by these two, they are called obstacles.
In the second stage, there is the ignorance of subtle transgressions and the ignorance of various paths of action; because one is deluded and submerged by these two, they are called obstacles.

In the third stage, there is the ignorance of seeking the Dharma and the ignorance regarding the fulfillment of the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retention; because one is deluded and submerged by these two, they are called obstacles.

In the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), there is the ignorance that craves meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the ignorance regarding the craving for dharmas; because one is deluded and submerged by these two, they are called hindrances.

In the fifth stage, there is the ignorance regarding mundane right mindfulness and reflection—which does not exclusively turn away from the world nor exclusively manifest the world—and the ignorance regarding supramundane right mindfulness and reflection—which does not exclusively turn away from nirvāṇa nor exclusively proceed toward nirvāṇa; because one is deluded and submerged by these two, they are called hindrances.

In the sixth stage, there is the ignorance regarding the manifestation of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) as they truly are, and the ignorance regarding the proliferation of various signs (*nimitta*); because one is deluded and submerged by these two, they are called hindrances.

Within the seventh stage, there is the ignorance of subtle characteristic-activity and the ignorance of one-sided contemplation of skillful means; because one is deluded and submerged by these two, they are called hindrances.

Within the eighth stage, there is the ignorance of the non-arising of spontaneous signlessness and the ignorance of not attaining mastery over all signs; because one is deluded and submerged by these two, they are called hindrances.

Within the ninth stage, there is the ignorance regarding the immeasurable preaching of Dharma, the immeasurable names and phrases, the supreme eloquence of wisdom, and the *dhāraṇī*, as well as the ignorance regarding the mastery of the eloquence of joyful speech; because one is deluded and submerged by these two, they are called hindrances.
Within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), there is the great pervasive ignorance and the entry into subtle, secret ignorance; because one is deluded and submerged by these two, they are called obstructions.

Within the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*), there is the extremely subtle ignorance regarding all objects and the ignorance that obstructs others; because one is deluded and submerged by these two, they are called obstructions.
“Lokêśvararāja! These are called the twenty-two kinds of ignorance and the eleven kinds of obstructions that explain the distinctions between the stages (*bhūmi*). Lokêśvararāja!”
"Yet this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is not associated with these various dharmas.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva said:
"It is rare, World-Honored One!"

Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi is of great benefit and great fruit; those bodhisattvas have shattered the net of great ignorance and delusion, and having also extinguished the dense forest of all false and opposing views, they attain Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!”
"What kinds of excellences are said to exist in these stages?
The Buddha said, "Avalokiteśvara!"
There are eight kinds of purity, namely:

purity of the straightforward mind, purity of loving-kindness, purity of compassion, purity of the perfections, purity of seeing and making offerings to all Buddhas, purity of teaching and transforming sentient beings, purity of birth, and purity of power.

“Lokanātha! Within the first stage (*bhūmi*), there is the purification of the straightforward mind (*ṛjukacitta*) up to the purification of power (*bala*). Furthermore, from the higher and higher stages up to the Buddha stage, there is the purification of the straightforward mind and the purification of power; one should know that these are purification, supreme purification, and superior purification.”

“Lokeśvara! Excluding the birth of purity in the Buddha-ground—that is, the various merits of the first ground, and those merits of all the grounds up to the highest of the high—those merits of the first ground are equal and without distinction; yet it should be known that each successive ground possesses superior merits.”
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason does the World-Honored One declare that, among all births, the birth of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is the most supreme?”
The Buddha said:
"Avalokiteśvara! There are four kinds of dharmas, namely:

Because they have perfectly accumulated and purified all roots of goodness; because they have attained skillful means regarding the internal mind; because they give rise to great compassion to rescue and protect all sentient beings; and because they themselves are undefiled, they are able to cause all sentient beings to be undefiled as well.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason does the World-Honored One say that all bodhisattvas are able to give rise to all manner of wondrous vows, supreme vows, and vows of extraordinary power?”
The Buddha said: “Avalokiteśvara!

There are four kinds of dharmas by which a bodhisattva can know the wondrous bliss of nirvāṇa as it truly is; thus they swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Furthermore, they are able to relinquish that swift attainment of the supreme and wondrous blissful practice for the sake of awakening, and they give rise to the great mind not for the sake of repaying a debt of gratitude, but for the benefit of sentient beings, undergoing all manner of various sufferings throughout the long night within the six realms.”
“Avalokiteśvara! For this reason, I speak of the wondrous vows, the supreme vows, and the vows of extraordinary power of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!
How many kinds of trainings are there for a bodhisattva mahāsattva?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: “Avalokiteśvara!
There are six kinds of training for a bodhisattva.”
What are the six?

They are the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā), the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Of these six kinds of training, how many constitute the training in higher ethical discipline?”
"How many are the trainings in higher mind (adhicittam-śikṣā)?
How many are the trainings in higher wisdom (adhiprajñām-śikṣā)? The Buddha said:

“Avalokiteśvara! The first three trainings—the *dānapāramitā*, *śīlapāramitā*, and *kṣāntipāramitā*—are the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*); the *dhyānapāramitā* is the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*); the *prajñāpāramitā* is the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajña-śikṣā*); and the *vīryapāramitā* pervades all the *pāramitās*.”
“Lokêśvara! You should know that three kinds of supremacy encompass six matters of training.
The Bodhisattva Lokêśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Of these six kinds of practice, how many are the adornment of merit,
and how many are the adornment of wisdom?”
The Buddha said: “Avalokiteśvara!

The adornment of the training in higher ethics is the merit-adornment; the adornment of the training in higher wisdom is the wisdom-adornment. You should know that the perfection of diligence and the perfection of meditation pervade all the perfections.”
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!”
"How should a bodhisattva train in these various trainings?
The Buddha said, "Avalokiteśvara!"
There are five modes of contemplation for training in these various trainings.
What are the five? They are:

teaching the Dharma based on the various pāramitās; relying on the Bodhisattva-piṭaka to first develop sincere faith; next, there are ten kinds of dharma-practice, through which one practices according to reality by means of the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation; and...
Because they protect the bodhicitta;
because they draw near to spiritual friends;
and because they practice all roots of goodness without ceasing.
"Avalokiteśvara! This is what is known as the bodhisattva’s training in all matters of study; you should understand it thus.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!
For what reason are these matters of training said to be six in number?”
The Buddha said,
“Avalokiteśvara! There are two kinds of meanings.”
What are these two? They are:
the gathering in of all sentient beings, and the counteracting of all obstacles. Avalokiteśvara!
The three types of training encompass sentient beings for their benefit, and the three types of training serve as remedies for all obstacles.
"Avalokiteśvara! When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), they encompass sentient beings by providing them with material necessities for their benefit."
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), they do not vex or harm others, gathering in sentient beings through the gift of fearlessness;
when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), they gather in sentient beings without any thought of seeking retribution for grievances.
"Āryavalokiteśvara! By means of these three trainings, one gathers in sentient beings. Āryavalokiteśvara!"

When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), they shake all afflictions (*kleśa*) and destroy all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); within the stage of practice, they are not moved by any affliction.
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), they bind all afflictions.
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), they sever all latent tendencies.
"Avalokiteśvara! These three pāramitās serve as the antidotes to the afflictions that are their opposites.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara to the Buddha.
“World-Honored One!
For what reason does the World-Honored One say that the other four pāramitās have only four numbers?
The Buddha said:
"Avalokiteśvara! For the sake of accomplishing those companions to the six pāramitās, the other four pāramitās are taught. Avalokiteśvara!"
The Bodhisattva’s three pāramitās gather in sentient beings; through the skillful means of gathering beings, they take them into wholesome dharmas.
For this reason, I say that the pāramitā of skillful means is the companion of the three pāramitās.

“Lokeśvara! When a bodhisattva manifests in a body whose mind is distracted by many afflictions and is thus unable to practice the Dharma as it truly is, yet still has faith and delight in limited practices and limited teachings, possesses a meagerly upright mind, and cannot grasp the right concentration of the inner mind; when they hear the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and contemplate it according to what they have heard, yet cannot enter meditative absorption and cannot give rise to supramundane wisdom, but instead cultivate the marks of the adornment of merit and wisdom in only small measure;
and when, relying on that small measure of the adornment of wisdom, they make vows to attenuate future afflictions—this is the bodhisattva’s perfection of vow (praṇidhāna-pāramitā).”
"I vow that in future lives my afflictions shall be thin and I may accomplish the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
For this reason, I say that the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*) is the companion of the perfection of diligence."

“Lokanātha! Because a bodhisattva draws near to spiritual friends, he hears the true Dharma, reflects upon it as it truly is, and is able to accord with it; by practicing according to reality, he turns away from that meager mind and increases the power of the wholesome. Within that realm of true suchness (tathatā-dharmadhātu), he attains superior power; this is the bodhisattva’s perfection of power (bala-pāramitā) which attains internal concentration.”
Therefore, I say that the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) is the companion of the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*). "Avalokiteśvara!

Because a bodhisattva relies upon the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, they correctly contemplate through the wisdom of hearing and cultivate the perfection of meditation; this is the bodhisattva’s perfection of knowledge (*jñāna-pāramitā*). Relying upon the perfection of knowledge, one is able to give rise to the supramundane perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*)."
"Therefore, I say that the perfection of wisdom (jñānapāramitā) is the companion of the perfection of prajñā.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“World-Honored One, for what reason do you teach the six pāramitās in this particular order?
The Buddha said, “Avalokiteśvara!
Because they progress through successive stages of increasing excellence,
Avalokiteśvara! A bodhisattva,
having distanced themselves from the mind of enjoying sensual desires, upholds the pure precepts;
Having undertaken and maintained the pure precepts, one is able to endure all evils;
having been able to endure all evils, one is able to achieve diligence;
having achieved diligence, one is able to enter the various dhyānas.
Once one is able to enter the various dhyānas, one is able to attain supramundane wisdom.
Avalokiteśvara! For this reason, I say that the six pāramitās should be understood according to this sequence.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many kinds of distinctions does the World-Honored One say there are for each of the pāramitās?”
The Buddha said:
"Avalokiteśvara! Each of the pāramitās has three distinct types of differentiation."
Avalokiteśvara! There are three kinds of dānapāramitā, namely: the gift of Dharma, the gift of material wealth, and the gift of fearlessness;
there are three kinds of śīlapāramitā, namely: the precept of abstaining from all unwholesome conduct, the precept of cultivating all wholesome conduct, and the precept of benefiting sentient beings.
The *kṣānti-pāramitā* has three kinds: namely, the patience of enduring all evils, the patience of enduring all sufferings, and the patience of enduring all dharmas;
the *vīrya-pāramitā* has three kinds: namely, the diligence of initiating effort, the diligence of practicing wholesome dharmas, and the diligence of benefiting sentient beings;

the *dhyāna-pāramitā* has three kinds: namely, the meditation of non-conceptual tranquility and supreme stillness that counteracts afflictions and experiences blissful practice, the meditation that gives rise to various merits, and the meditation that gives rise to the benefit of sentient beings.

There are three kinds of Prajñāpāramitā: namely, the Prajñā that contemplates conventional truth, the Prajñā that contemplates ultimate truth, and the Prajñā that contemplates the benefit of sentient beings.
“Avalokiteśvara! You should know that these are called the three types of distinctions for each of the pāramitās of all dharmas.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
for what reason are the various pāramitās called ‘pāramitās’?
The Buddha said:
“Avalokiteśvara! There are five meanings by which they are called pāramitās: namely, non-attachment, lack of expectation, faultlessness, non-discrimination, and dedication.”
Avalokiteśvara! "Non-attachment" refers to not being attached to things that are contrary to the various pāramitās;
"lack of expectation" means having no seeking mind regarding the enjoyment of the fruits of the pāramitās or the repayment of their benefits.
"Being without fault" means being far removed from the defiled dharmas that lack skillful means regarding the various *pāramitās*.
"Non-discrimination" means not adhering to the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the various *pāramitās* as they were heard.
"Dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*) means dedicating whatever has been performed and accumulated through the various *pāramitās* toward the fruit of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
"Avalokiteśvara! For this reason, I say they are called 'pāramitās'.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many kinds of things are there that are contrary to the various pāramitās?
The Buddha said:
“Avalokiteśvara! There are six kinds of things that are contrary to the pāramitās. What are these six?
That is to say, it is because one delights in the mastery over the requisites for the five desires; because one experiences the mastery over seeing the merit and benefits;
because one exercises mastery over the conduct of body, speech, and mind;
and because one cannot endure the slighting or harming of others.
Because they are attached to their own personal pleasure;
because they are single-mindedly intent on worldly distracted activities;
and because within the world they regard names, concepts, and discriminations—which they have seen, heard, sensed, and known—as superior merits.
"Avalokiteśvara! These are called the things that are contrary to the various pāramitās.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!
What is the fruit and retribution of the various pāramitās?”
The Buddha said:
"Avalokiteśvara! You should know that there are six kinds of karmic fruits and rewards resulting from the various pāramitās."

What are the six? They are: attaining abundant wealth; proceeding toward the good realms; being without enemies; possessing unimpaired and manifold joy and happiness; constantly serving as a lord for sentient beings; not harming one's own person; and possessing great majestic power.
"Avalokiteśvara! These are called the six kinds of fruits and rewards of the pāramitās.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are the defiled dharmas of the various pāramitās?
The Buddha said:
“Avalokiteśvara! There are four kinds of unrighteous practice regarding the pāramitās, which are termed ‘defilement. What are these four?
"It is because they act without a mind of loving-kindness, because they act without right mindfulness, because they do not cease unwholesome conduct, and because they act without a sincere heart.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“What is improper reflection? The Buddha said, “Lokeshvara!”
"To practice the various pāramitās while remaining apart from the practice of the other pāramitās is called incorrect reflection.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
“What, then, is the bodhisattva’s practice without skillful means?
The Buddha said, “Avalokiteśvara!

If a bodhisattva, while practicing the perfections to gather in sentient beings, satisfies them merely with the pleasures of food, drink, and material requisites, yet fails to cause them to leave unwholesome states and establish them in wholesome states, this is called the bodhisattva’s practice without skillful means.
Why is this? Avalokiteśvara!
It is not the giving of food, drink, and such pleasures that is called "benefit."
Avalokiteśvara! For example, whether it be much or little, no one can cause excrement and filth to produce a fragrant and sweet scent. Avalokiteśvara!

Thus, all conditioned phenomena are characterized by suffering, and all sentient beings are inherently subject to various forms of suffering; food, drink, and the requisites for life that sustain sentient beings cannot be considered true happiness.

Avalokiteśvara! If one establishes sentient beings within the state of ultimate bliss—the foremost and supreme among all wholesome dharmas—it is called "gathering them in" and bestowing great benefit upon them.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!”
“How many kinds of purity do these pāramitās possess?
The Buddha said, “Avalokiteśvara!
I do not say that there is any purity apart from these five kinds of purity.
Avalokiteśvara! It is based on these five kinds of purity that I have briefly and extensively explained the characteristics of the purity of the various pāramitās.
“Lokêśvara! What is the mark of the brief explanation of the purity of the various pāramitās? Lokêśvara!”
All perfections possess seven kinds of purity.
What are these seven? They are as follows:
namely, that a bodhisattva teaches the Dharma while remaining detached from a self-concept, and furthermore, because they do not seek wisdom from others.
This vision does not give rise to attachment toward any phenomena, because it knows that all phenomena can grasp great Bodhi;
it does not give rise to divergent thoughts or divergent doubts;
and it neither praises itself nor disparages others.
Because they do not deceive, are not arrogant, and are not negligent;
because they do not give rise to a sense of complacency upon attaining even a small amount of wholesome dharmas;
and because, having attained these various dharmas, they do not give rise to envy or stinginess toward others.
"Ārya Avalokiteśvara!
These are the seven kinds of purity of all the pāramitās that should be known;
this is their brief explanation. Ārya Avalokiteśvara!"
I shall further explain in detail the characteristics of the purity of the various pāramitās; based on those seven kinds, I shall explain the purity of the various pāramitās.
What are these seven kinds?
Avalokiteśvara! I speak of the seven kinds of purity in the dānapāramitā of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, which they practice according to reality.
What are these seven?

That which is called giving with a mind of compassion is purity of giving; purity of giving is purity of precepts, purity of view, purity of mind, purity of speech, purity of wisdom, and purity of intention.
These are known as the seven kinds of purity of the *dānapāramitā*;
one should understand them thus. "Avalokiteśvara!
In this way, there are seven kinds of purity of the *śīlapāramitā*."
What are the seven? They are as follows:

a bodhisattva mahāsattva upholds the precepts received by a bodhisattva; knows all precepts as they truly are; is able to know, as they truly are, the dharmas that are free from faults; constantly maintains those dharmas with firm precepts, sincere precepts, and precepts that are always in accordance [with the Dharma]; and upholds the precepts as they truly are among all the trainings.
"Avalokiteśvara! These are called the seven kinds of purity of the perfection of ethical discipline;
you should know this. Avalokiteśvara!"
In this way, the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) has seven kinds of purity.
What are these seven? They are as follows:
the bodhisattva, having personal conviction in the retribution of karma, does not harbor anger or resentment toward any harmful actions.
Whether reviled, angered, or beaten, even when all manner of evil deeds are inflicted upon his person, he does not give rise to a mind of retaliation nor harbor resentment;
if the other seeks repentance, he accepts it immediately without causing them further distress;
he practices patience not out of seeking something from others, nor out of fear, nor for the sake of food and drink.
Not forgetting to repay the kindness received from others— O Avalokiteśvara!
This should be known as the sevenfold purity of the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
"Avalokiteśvara! There are seven kinds of purity in the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*). What are these seven?

It is said that a bodhisattva knows diligence as it truly is because of its equality; because they do not exalt themselves or disparage others on account of their diligence; because their body abides peacefully and immovable like a mountain; because they are constantly and diligently energetic; because their mind is not timid or weak; because their conduct is firm and steadfast; and because they give rise to a mind of diligence toward all wholesome dharmas without rest.
"O Avalokiteśvara! These are known as the seven kinds of purity of the *vīryapāramitā*;
you should understand them thus. O Avalokiteśvara!"
The dhyānapāramitā has seven kinds of purity. What are the seven? They are:

the dhyānapāramitā of the samādhi of the Bodhisattva’s well-determined knowledge of all marks; the dhyānapāramitā of the fulfillment of samādhi; the dhyānapāramitā of the samādhi that knows the two parts as they truly are; the dhyānapāramitā of the samādhi that proceeds in accordance with reality as it truly is; the dhyānapāramitā of the samādhi that does not rely [on anything]; the dhyānapāramitā of the samādhi that is well-trained in the wholesome actions performed through various activities; and the dhyānapāramitā of the immeasurable samādhis of the Bodhisattvapitaka.
"Avalokiteśvara! These are the seven kinds of purity of the dhyānapāramitā that should be known. Avalokiteśvara!"
The Prajñāpāramitā possesses seven kinds of purity.
What are these seven? They are as follows:

being free from the slanders of existence and non-existence; the Middle Way Prajñā; and, by relying on the power of Prajñā, being able to know the meanings of the three gates of liberation—namely, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—exactly as they are.
One can know, as they truly are, the three types:
the imagined, the dependent, and the ultimate truth;
one can know, as they truly are, these three types:
The intrinsic nature of the characteristics of names, the characteristics of arising, and the characteristics of the ultimate truth;
knowing the five fields of knowledge according to worldly convention as they truly are;
and knowing the ultimate truth as it truly is.
One does not engage in conceptualization or discursive proliferation regarding the seven kinds of suchness;
rather, one extensively cultivates the single flavor of immeasurable differentiated contemplations of phenomena, śamatha, and vipaśyanā,
thereby achieving accomplishment through practice in accordance with what has been heard as it truly is.
"Avalokiteśvara! These are known as the seven kinds of purity of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!
Regarding these five kinds of contemplation, what are the respective functions of each individual contemplation?”
The Buddha said:
“Avalokiteśvara! You should know that each of these five kinds of contemplation has five functions.”
What are these five? They are:
that a bodhisattva does not cling to present rewards, because they constantly practice the various pāramitās with a sincere mind and are free from negligence;
and they do not hope for gratitude in return, because they embrace the future and are free from negligence.
They are free from all faults because they are able to excellently fulfill, excellently purify, and excellently cleanse the various *pāramitās*;
they swiftly fulfill the various *pāramitās* by relying on non-conceptual skillful means;

and by the power of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), they obtain excellent karmic fruits in all places of birth, and by relying on that, they practice the various *pāramitās* as they truly are without exhaustion, until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Lokêśvara! This is what should be known as the distinct activities of the various pāramitās of a bodhisattva.
Thus addressed, the Bodhisattva Lokêśvara said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!
Among these various pāramitās, which one is the most supreme?”
The Buddha said:
"Avalokiteśvara! It is that which consists of not being stingy with material wealth, not clinging to karmic rewards, and dedicating [merit] toward great enlightenment, Avalokiteśvara!"
"This is what should be known as the most supreme. Avalokiteśvara said,
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the dharma that is without defilement?
The Buddha said:
"That which is free from all faults and free from conceptual discrimination—this should be known as the dharma without defilement."
Avalokiteśvara said: “World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘luminous and subtle’?”
The Buddha said:
"One should know that which is called the cessation of all dharmas through conditions.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!
What is the Bodhisattva’s Immovable Ground?”
The Buddha said, “Avalokiteśvara!
When a bodhisattva enters the first stage, the Stage of Joy, they become endowed with great power and do not regress from any dharmas; this should be known as the bodhisattva’s Immovable Stage.”
Avalokiteśvara said: “World-Honored One!
What dharma is the dharma of perfect purity?”
The Buddha said:
"One should know that this refers to the fulfillment of the ten stages (bhūmis) up to the fulfillment of the stage of Buddhahood.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!
For what reason do the bodhisattvas' various pāramitās never come to an end, and their delight in the fruits of retribution also never comes to an end?”
The Buddha said:
“It should be understood that what is called ‘mutually dependent arising’ refers to the production of sublime fruits.
*Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, Scroll Four.
The Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Part Two of the Chapter on the Questions of the Holy Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
The noble Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!”
"For what reason, World-Honored One, do the bodhisattvas not take great delight in the retributive fruits of the pāramitās, but instead take great delight in the practice of the pāramitās?
The Buddha said, "Avalokiteśvara!"
There are five kinds of dharmas. What are the five? They are:

because one delights in the joy of spiritual excellence; because one gathers for oneself the benefit of both self and others; because one delights in the future retribution of happiness as a repayment of kindness; because one is undefiled by all phenomena; and because one does not lose those dharmas—this should be known.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!”
“World-Honored One, how many kinds of supreme and wondrous powers do each of these pāramitās possess?
The Buddha said, “Avalokiteśvara!
It should be understood that each of these perfections possesses four kinds of sublime power. What are these four?

First, it means that when a bodhisattva practices the various perfections, they remain far removed from a mind of stinginess and envy, a mind of broken precepts, a mind of anger, a mind of laziness, a mind of distraction, and a mind of various [wrong] views.
Because it can accomplish all the merits of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
because it manifests in person to encompass both one's own body and the bodies of others;
and because in future lives it can obtain the vast and inexhaustible fruit of love.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!”
Regarding these perfections (pāramitās), what constitutes their cause?
What constitutes their fruit?
And what constitutes their power?
The Buddha said:
“Avalokiteśvara! You should know that great compassion is the cause, the joyful gathering-in of sentient beings is the fruit, and the ability to fulfill bodhi is the power.”
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!”

If all the material resources of bodhisattvas are inexhaustible when used according to their will, and these bodhisattvas furthermore possess a heart of great compassion, for what reason do the impoverished sentient beings in the world undergo such various sufferings?
The Buddha said:
"Avalokiteśvara! These sentient beings [suffer] due to the transgressions of their own karma."

The great compassion of a bodhisattva constantly desires to bestow inexhaustible wealth and happiness upon all sentient beings; it is ever-present with pity and is firm and unshakable. Avalokiteśvara!
If all sentient beings were free from their own karmic obstacles, there would be no impoverished beings in the world. "Avalokiteśvara!
It is as if all hungry ghosts, tormented by thirst, go to see all the rivers and great oceans, only to find them completely dried up."
This is not the fault of the rivers or the great ocean; rather, it is the retribution for the evil karma committed by the hungry ghosts themselves.
When Bodhisattvas bestow all manner of necessities upon sentient beings, they are like that great ocean, free from any fault.

Yet when sentient beings suffer the misery of poverty, it is because they have created such evil karma for themselves—just as those hungry ghosts receive their retribution—and it is not the fault of the Bodhisattvas.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!”
“Bodhisattva, by which pāramitā does one grasp that all dharmas have no intrinsic nature?
The Buddha said, “Avalokiteśvara!”
"The Prajñāpāramitā grasps all dharmas as being without essence or characteristics. Avalokiteśvara said:
"World-Honored One!"
If, World-Honored One, the bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā grasps all dharmas as being without intrinsic nature or characteristics,
for what reason does prajñāpāramitā not grasp all dharmas as having intrinsic nature or characteristics?
The Buddha said, “Avalokiteśvara!
I speak of grasping as being without intrinsic nature; regarding that which is without intrinsic nature, you should not become attached to words.”

Why is this? Because the dharma that is without intrinsic nature transcends all names and language; it is a dharma realized within one's own body, which cannot be expressed through names or phrases. It is by relying on names that I say that Prajñāpāramitā grasps the fact that all dharmas are without intrinsic nature.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the World-Honored One has spoken of the various pāramitās, the proximate pāramitās, and the great pāramitās.”
World-Honored One!
What is a pāramitā? What is a near-pāramitā?
"What is the Great Pāramitā?
The Buddha said, "Avalokiteśvara!"

From immeasurable kalpas, the Bodhisattva practices the various pāramitās such as giving and ultimately attains all wholesome dharmas. Although that Bodhisattva possesses the nature of afflictions which manifest within the mind, those afflictions cannot defile the Bodhisattva, and the Bodhisattva is able to subdue them—this refers to the stage of practice through faith (śraddhā-carita-bhūmi). Cultivating all practices with a degree of faith that is weak or middling is called a pāramitā.

“Lokêśvara! Furthermore, there are those who have practiced the superior wholesome dharmas for immeasurable kalpas, yet whose mental activities are still governed by afflictions; nevertheless, those bodhisattvas are able to subdue the afflictions, and the afflictions cannot overcome them—this should be understood as referring to those who have not yet entered the first bhūmi, Lokêśvara!”
This is called the proximate pāramitā. Furthermore, Avalokiteśvara!

A bodhisattva practices the supreme and sublime dharmas throughout immeasurable kalpas; in that bodhisattva, no afflictions whatsoever arise in the mind—namely, from the first bhūmi through the eighth bhūmi up to the tenth bhūmi.
"Avalokiteśvara! This is what is called the Great Pāramitā; you should know it as such.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!
How many kinds of latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) are there within these stages?”
The Buddha said:
"Avalokiteśvara! There are three kinds of latent afflictions (*anuśaya*)."
What are these three? They are:
the latent afflictions that destroy their companions, the latent afflictions that are attenuated, and the subtle latent afflictions. Avalokiteśvara!
What are the afflictions that destroy their own companions?
These refer to the non-innate afflictions from the first stage through the fifth stage.

Innate afflictions accompany those bodhisattvas; because the afflictions that destroy their companions do not operate within their minds, I therefore speak of "afflictions that destroy their companions."
Avalokiteśvara! What are the subtle latent afflictions?
They are the subtle latent afflictions of ignorance within the sixth and seventh stages.
When a bodhisattva practices and thins out those afflictions of ignorance, this is called "thinned-out latent afflictions" (tanu-kleśānuśaya). Avalokiteśvara!
What are the subtle and extremely subtle afflictions?

This refers to the eighth stage and the stages above it, wherein all latent tendencies of ignorance and afflictions no longer function within the mind; there remains only the subtle obstruction regarding all objective spheres.
"Avalokiteśvara! These are known as the three kinds of latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) that should be understood.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One has said that when a bodhisattva severs all faults, they attain the severance of all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
World-Honored One!”
“By severing how many kinds of faults is a bodhisattva said to have severed all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)?
The Buddha said, “Avalokiteśvara!”
The Bodhisattva severs three kinds of faults and is thus able to sever all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). What are these three?
They are the skin, the flesh, and the bone.

Avalokiteśvara! First, by severing the obstruction of the skin, one leaves behind the first fault; next, by severing the obstruction of the flesh, one leaves behind the second fault; next, by severing the obstruction of the bone, one leaves behind the third fault. I declare that the total exhaustion of all latent tendencies (anuśaya) is to be known as the stage of a Buddha (buddhabhūmi).
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!”
“For how many asaṃkhyeya kalpas will those various faults be severed?
The Buddha said, “Avalokiteśvara!”

It should be understood that throughout three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas—during immeasurable times, immeasurable months, immeasurable half-months, immeasurable nights, immeasurable days, immeasurable moments of thought, immeasurable *kṣaṇas*, immeasurable *muhūrtas*, and immeasurable *lava* kalpas—one must sever all those faults.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what are the characteristics of the afflictions of these bodhisattvas within these stages?”
"What merits does it possess?
I pray that you will explain them to me, so that I may understand.
The Buddha said:
“Avalokiteśvara! You should know that afflictions do not arise from the appearance of stained characteristics; rather, afflictions arise from immeasurable merits. Why is this?

In the first stage (*bhūmi*), the bodhisattva personally realizes the intrinsic nature of the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and is well able to awaken to and know that entire realm of phenomena.
Therefore, the bodhisattva is able to know, as it truly is, the arising of all afflictions; it is not that they do not know them.
Therefore, within one's own being there is no characteristic of defilement, because it cannot give rise to the faults of various sufferings;
and since there are no such faults, for the sake of severing cause and effect within the realm of sentient beings, the immeasurable merits of a bodhisattva arise from afflictions.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara said:
“How rare, World-Honored One!

This Great Bodhi is able to bring about such great benefit; for it causes the afflictions of all bodhisattvas to subdue all the roots of goodness of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, let alone all other immeasurable merits.”
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
As the World-Honored One has taught, the Śrāvaka Vehicle and the Mahāyāna constitute a single vehicle."
“World-Honored One!
With what intention do you speak thus?
The Buddha said:

“Avalokiteśvara! Within my Śrāvaka vehicle, I teach various dharmas—namely, the five aggregates, the six internal bases, and the six external bases—and yet I declare that such dharmas as these are of a single flavor within the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), which those śrāvakas are unable to realize.”
Therefore, I speak of various vehicles. Avalokiteśvara!

If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing such teachings, engage in conceptual discrimination and attachment, those people do not understand the essence of the One Vehicle; they grasp at various vehicles to realize that Dharma, seizing them as distinct and different, and thus fall into mutual contention.
"You should know that this is my intention.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The various characteristics of all phenomena, I explain based on a single principle."
Those who give rise to inferior understanding, I call them followers of the two vehicles.
Like those who discriminate based on what they hear without knowing its true meaning,
the various vehicles conflict with one another, and thus arrogant beings engage in dispute.
"Knowing the sublime characteristics of the stages, And the places of rebirth resulting from vows—
This supreme counteragent, I declare to be the Mahāyāna. At that time,
the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, what is the name of this dharma-gate?
How should it be upheld?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: “Avalokiteśvara!
This sūtra is titled ‘The Dharma Gate of the Definitive Meaning of the Grounds and Perfections’; you should now receive and uphold it in this manner.”
When this *Sūtra of the Definitive Meaning of the Bhūmi-pāramitā* was being taught, seventy-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the Mahāyāna-āloka-samādhi.

Chapter Eleven: The Inquiry of the Noble Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta Bodhisattva (Part Five). At that time, the noble Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, relying upon the distinctions in the activities of the Tathāgata’s sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*), addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“World-Honored One!
What are the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"By practicing the ten stages and the pāramitās as they truly are, one transforms the body and achieves the attainment of the sublime Dharma-body; this is what should be known as the correspondence with the Dharma-body of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas."
“Mañjuśrī! That Buddha’s Dharma-body has two kinds of inconceivable characteristics. What are these two?

That which is called the Dharma-body is free from all conceptual proliferation (prapañca) and free from all conditioned characteristics (saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa), yet sentient beings cling to conceptual proliferation and conditioned characteristics.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is that which is attained by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas upon the transformation of their bodies the Dharma-body?”
"Is it the non-Dharma-body?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī,
"It is not the non-Dharma-body."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If it is not the Dharma-body, what kind of body is it?”
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! It is called the liberation-body, not the dharma-body.”
Based on the body of liberation, the bodies of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all Tathāgatas are equal; however, there is a distinction and superiority regarding the Dharma-body.

As for the excellence of the Dharma-body, it surpasses the immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits of all those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; its extraordinary and sublime nature is beyond all analogy.
"To provide a remedy for the discrimination of perversions, that person speaks of the birth of the Tathāgata.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What are the characteristics of the Buddhas' birth in the world? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"The characteristics of the birth of the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) correspond to the characteristics of the world; it is endowed with the characteristics of being sustained by all kinds of adornments of every merit. This is to be understood as the correspondence of the transformation body's birth in the world."
“Mañjuśrī! The Dharma-body of the Buddha-Tathāgata is unborn.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should I understand the manifested signs of skillful means performed by the transformation body?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"In all Buddha-lands, within the great trichiliocosm, those from families of great power and families that are fields of merit simultaneously descend, enter the womb, dwell in the womb, emerge from the womb, and having been born, grow; they experience the pleasures of the five senses, yet practice great renunciation, leave the home life, perform austerities, realize enlightenment, turn the wheel of Dharma, and enter nirvana."
“Mañjuśrī! You should know that these are the skillful means manifested by the emanation body.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!

By the sustaining power of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, how many kinds of speech does the Tathāgata employ to preach the Dharma for sentient beings—how does the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma rely upon those who can be transformed, maturing those who are not yet matured, and bringing those already matured to liberation?”
The Buddha said:
"Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata has three kinds of speech."
What are these three?
They are the teaching of the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā. Mañjuśrī!
"These are the three kinds that should be known. Mañjuśrī said:
"World-Honored One!"
What is the Sūtra? What is the Vinaya? What is the Mātṛkā?
The Buddha said:
"Mañjuśrī! That which I have taught as the Dharma of few matters is called a sūtra."
Regarding the Dharma of few matters, it refers to four kinds of matters, nine kinds of matters, and twenty-nine kinds of matters.

"Mañjuśrī! As for what are called the four kinds of matters, they are: the matter of hearing, the matter of taking refuge, the matter of training, and the matter of awakening; these are named the four kinds of matters."

“Mañjuśrī! As for what are called the nine kinds of things, they are: the thing of designation; the thing of sentient beings tending toward enjoyment; the thing of tending toward birth; the thing of tending toward abiding in birth; the thing of tending toward defilement and purification; the thing of tending toward diversity; the thing of the speaker; the thing of that which is spoken; and the thing of the retinue. These are called the nine kinds of things.”
“Mañjuśrī! What are called the twenty-nine matters refer to the matters that accord with the activities of the afflictions in relation to the defiled.
What are these matters that accord?
This refers to conforming to the characteristics of that person;

it concerns the causal factors for birth in future lives, the causal factors for future activity based on the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), the objects of observation belonging to the pure portion (*śubhabhāga*), and the practice of cultivation at those very points.
The objects for which the mind abides are: the object of experiencing happiness in the present life, and the object of observing the transcendence of all suffering.
One knows these objects as they truly are. "Those objects are of three kinds:

because they are sustained by dwelling in perversion; because they are sustained by the characteristics of external false practice based on the mark of the notion of a sentient being; and because they are sustained by an internal mind free from pride."
Regarding the matters of abiding in practice, the matter of direct realization, the matter of practice, and the matter of establishing firm application, one contemplates those nine types of matters:

the matter of observing the means of being secluded or not secluded; the matter of tending toward distraction; the matter of non-distraction and non-loss; the matter of unimpeded practice; the matter of beneficial practice; the matter of firm application; the matter of tending toward that actual realization; and the matter of attaining parinirvāṇa in its fullness.

“The Tathāgata has well expounded the Dharma of the Vinaya—the right view of the world—which excels all the superior matters of the various non-Buddhists; one does not regress from that Dharma through failing to practice it.”
Why is this? Mañjuśrī!
If one is unable to practice within the well-expounded Dharma of the Vinaya of the Tathāgata, causing wholesome qualities to decline, this is not the fault of wrong views.
Mañjuśrī said: “World-Honored One!
What is the characteristic of the Vinaya?”

“Mañjuśrī! As for the characteristics of the Vinaya, when I teach the Prātimokṣa and the dharmas associated with the Prātimokṣa for the sake of the śrāvakas and all bodhisattvas, this is called the matter of the Vinaya.”
Mañjuśrī said: “World-Honored One!
How many kinds of dharmas does a bodhisattva have that encompass the prātimokṣa?”
The Buddha said:
"Mañjuśrī, there are seven kinds of dharmas by which a bodhisattva embraces the prātimokṣa."

What are these seven? They are: the Bodhisattva’s knowledge of explaining the dharmas to be upheld; knowledge of explaining matters concerning the *pārājika* offenses; knowledge of explaining matters concerning transgressions; knowledge of explaining the nature of matters that constitute transgressions; knowledge of explaining the nature of matters that do not constitute transgressions; knowledge of explaining matters concerning the arising of transgressions; and knowledge of explaining matters concerning the loss of the dharmas to be upheld.
“Mañjuśrī! These are known as the seven dharmas by which a bodhisattva’s prātimokṣa is subsumed;
this should be understood. Mañjuśrī said:
“World-Honored One!
What is the Mātṛkā? “Mañjuśrī! [the Buddha replied.]
“The elevenfold characteristics of the definitive sūtras that I have taught are called the *mātṛkā*. Mañjuśrī said,
“World-Honored One!”
"What are the eleven characteristics of the Mātṛkā? The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!"

Namely: the characteristic of conventional truth, the characteristic of ultimate truth, the characteristic of observing the factors of enlightenment, the characteristic of those phenomena, the characteristic of their intrinsic nature, the characteristic of the fruit of those phenomena, the characteristic of receiving the teaching of those phenomena, the characteristic of obstacles to those phenomena, the characteristic of conformity to those phenomena, the characteristic of faults in those phenomena, and the characteristic of benefits of those phenomena.
Mañjuśrī said: "World-Honored One! What is the characteristic of conventional truth?"
“Mañjuśrī! There are three kinds of characteristics of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya). What are these three?

"One should understand that it refers to the characteristics of persons, the characteristics of the essence of discrimination, and the characteristics of performing various types of karmic actions through the contemplation and reflection upon all phenomena. Mañjuśrī said:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)? "Mañjuśrī,
there are seven kinds of characteristics of the ultimate truth, as explained previously among the seven kinds of suchness (*tathatā*):"
First is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the characteristics of beginningless conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*);
second is the ultimate truth of characteristics, namely the emptiness of self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*);
third is the ultimate truth of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*), which is the knowledge that conditioned phenomena are nothing but mind and consciousness.
Fourth is the ultimate truth of attachment, which is what I call the truth of suffering;
fifth is the ultimate truth of wrong practice, which is what I call the truth of origination;
sixth is the ultimate truth of purification, which is what I call the truth of cessation.
Seventh, the correct practice of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which I call the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*). "Mañjuśrī!

The ultimate truth of phenomenal characteristics, the ultimate truth of attachment, and the ultimate truth of wrong practice—these three types of ultimate truth are equal and without distinction for all sentient beings."
Mañjuśrī! The ultimate truth of characteristics and the ultimate truth of consciousness-only—these two ultimate truths are equal in all phenomena, without distinction.
Mañjuśrī! The pure ultimate truth is equal and without distinction for śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of bodhisattvas.

“Mañjuśrī! One who correctly practices the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) should understand that, according to the distinctions of the sublime Dharma as it was heard, one contemplates śamatha and vipaśyanā so as to embrace the equality and non-differentiation of the prajñāpāramitā.”
Mañjuśrī said: “World-Honored One! What is the characteristic of contemplating the factors of enlightenment?”
“Mañjuśrī! One who contemplates the characteristics of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) should know that this means contemplating all types of phenomena. Mañjuśrī said:
“World-Honored One!
What is the characteristic of those dharmas? “Mañjuśrī!”
"That characteristic of phenomena should be understood as it is presented in the eightfold contemplation. Mañjuśrī said,
"World-Honored One!"
"What are the eight kinds of contemplation? Mañjuśrī, they are:

that which relies on the truth of reality, the truth of abiding, faults, merits, common characteristics, specific characteristics, characteristics of correspondence, and characteristics of extensive and concise exposition."
“Mañjuśrī! The characteristic of ultimate truth is what is called *tathatā* (suchness).

The characteristics of abiding in truth are what are called: the characteristic of the personal self (*pudgala-lakṣaṇa*); the characteristic of answering categorically regarding the nature of distinctions and classifications; the characteristic of answering by way of analysis according to the question; the characteristic of setting aside the question (*sthāpanīya-praśna*); and the characteristic of manifesting secret matters.”
"The characteristic of faults refers to what I call the defiled transgressions of all phenomena.
The characteristic of merits refers to what I call the characteristic of the immeasurable benefits of all pure phenomena."
“Regarding the general characteristics, six kinds should be known.
What are these six? They are:

the penetration of the true meaning, the penetration of attainment, the penetration of teaching, the penetration of departing from the two extremes, the penetration of the inconceivable, and the penetration of intention.”
“Regarding ‘characteristics’ (*lakṣaṇa*), these refer to the three characteristics of the three periods of time, the three conditioned characteristics, and the four kinds of causal conditions.
Regarding ‘corresponding characteristics’ (*sābhisaṃskāra-lakṣaṇa*), there are four kinds that should be known.”
What are the four? They are:
the correlation of mutual dependence, the correlation of agent and action, the correlation of arising, and the correlation of the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Regarding the correlation of mutual dependence: what causes and what conditions are able to produce the functions of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), names, and so forth? This is called the correlation of mutual dependence.

Regarding the correspondence between the agent and the action: what causes and what conditions can acquire a phenomenon and produce a phenomenon; once the phenomenon has been produced, they can accomplish its function—this is called the correspondence between the agent and the action.

Regarding "correspondence with arising" (*jāti-saṃprayukta*): it refers to knowing the Dharma, teaching the Dharma, and demonstrating the Dharma through whatever causes and whatever conditions; being able to accomplish and correctly awaken to this is called correspondence with arising.
Regarding the correspondence of the dharma-body, there are briefly two kinds.
What are these two? They are: first, purity; second, impurity.
“Mañjuśrī! There are five characteristics of purity and seven characteristics of impurity. Mañjuśrī!”
What are the five aspects of purity? First, the aspect of direct perception;

second, the aspect based on that direct perception; third, the aspect of specific characteristics and analogies; fourth, the aspect of accomplishment; and fifth, the aspect of explaining the pure Āgamas.
“Mañjuśrī! What is that mark of direct perception?

It refers to such things as the direct perception of phenomena in the world, namely: ‘All conditioned formations are impermanent,’ ‘All conditioned formations are suffering,’ and ‘All phenomena are without self. This is what should be known as the mark of direct perception.”
“Mañjuśrī! What is the characteristic of seeing that which is present before one?
It is because all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) have a single characteristic, and thus one does not lose future wholesome or unwholesome karma.”

Based on the direct perception of those coarse phenomena, based on the direct perception of various sentient beings as they appear through various karmas, and based on the direct perception of experiencing suffering and pleasure due to wholesome and unwholesome karma—these serve as analogies within the context of directly perceived phenomena.
In this way, those based on direct perception should be understood accordingly.
"Mañjuśrī! As for the characteristics of internal and external analogies, these refer to the causes and conditions of analogies directly perceived within and without the entire world."
These and others like them should be understood as the characteristics of intrinsic nature, causes, conditions, and analogies.

Thus, that which relies upon those directly perceived characteristics, depends upon those directly perceived characteristics, and establishes a matter through the characteristic of an analogy in an entirely consistent manner is called "establishment by correspondence"; this should be understood.
“Mañjuśrī! What is the characteristic of the teaching of the pure Āgamas?
It is the characteristic of that tranquil nirvāṇa as taught by the Omniscient One.”
These and others like them should be understood as the pure Āgamas.

"Mañjuśrī! You should thus deeply observe the five kinds of pure characteristics. Having deeply observed them and known their purity, and having known their purity, you should practice that which is to be known."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How many kinds of dharmas are there by which one knows the marks of an omniscient person?"
The Buddha said:
"Mañjuśrī! There are five kinds of dharmas by which one knows the marks of an omniscient person."

What are these five? There is one who appears in the world and is called "All-Knowing" by all the worlds of devas and humans; there is one who ultimately accomplishes the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, attains the ten powers (*daśabala*) and is able to sever the doubts of all sentient beings; there is one who possesses the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), subdues all Māras and hostile adversaries, and in teaching the Dharma, none can create obstacles or difficulties; there is one who, within the teaching of the Dharma, skillfully explains the eightfold noble path of enlightenment (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*); and there is one who realizes and accomplishes the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.

“Mañjuśrī! Thus, by relying on arising and relying on characteristics, one cuts off doubt and achieves subjugation; no one is able to challenge this. When the five dharmas of a śramaṇa are seen manifest before one, this should be known as being in correspondence with an omniscient person.”

“Mañjuśrī! This is based on the correspondence of origination, the correspondence of direct perception, the correspondence of valid cognition, the correspondence of inferential knowledge, and the correspondence of the Dharma-teachings of the noble ones; knowing these five kinds of characteristics is called ‘knowing the correspondence of purity.’”
“Mañjuśrī! What are the seven kinds of impure characteristics? They are:

the characteristic of seeing similarity, the characteristic of seeing dissimilarity, the characteristic of having all similarities, the characteristic of having all dissimilarities, the characteristic of a different analogy for oneself, the characteristic of non-establishment, and the characteristic of impure scriptural transmission (āgama) regarding the teaching of the Dharma.”
“Mañjuśrī! What is the characteristic of the similar appearance of all things?

It refers to the fact that all phenomena are known through the mental consciousness as having the same characteristic; such instances are called the characteristic of the similar and identical appearance of all phenomena.”
“Mañjuśrī! What is the characteristic of all phenomena being seen as dissimilar?

It refers to the characteristic of dharmas, the characteristic of essence, the distinct characteristics of the causes and effects of karmic dharmas, individual characteristics, differing characteristics, ultimate mutual characteristics, and characteristics of relative dependence; such as these are called the characteristics of all things being dissimilar and seen as different.”
“Mañjuśrī! What is the characteristic of dissimilarity in self-illustration?

It refers to the fact that within those illustrations of similar appearances, there exist all manner of dissimilar and discordant characteristics; because these fail to establish the matter in question in a definitive way, I call them the characteristic of non-establishment.”

“Mañjuśrī! Within the analogies themselves, there exist characteristics of dissimilarity as well as all characteristics of similarity and commonality; because these fail to establish that matter in any way whatsoever, I therefore speak of the characteristic of non-establishment.”
"If a characteristic is not established, that dharma is not pure;
if a dharma is not pure, it should not be practiced.
Therefore, I say that the characteristic of the *āgama* is impure, and one should know this because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is impure."
“Mañjuśrī! What is the essence of phenomena?
It is as follows:”

"Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear in the world, the persistence of phenomena (dharma-sthiti), the essence of phenomena (dharma-tattva), and the realm of phenomena (dharma-dhātu)—these are to be known as the correspondence with the essence of phenomena. Mañjuśrī said:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the characteristic of the concise and the extensive? Mañjuśrī, it is as follows:

what is called a single phrase in brief—that single phrase, the superior phrase, the infinitely differentiated phrases, and even the teaching on the destination to which one should go—is to be known as the concise exposition."
Mañjuśrī said: “World-Honored One, what is the characteristic of attainment?”

“Mañjuśrī! When one grasps the views regarding all phenomena and contemplates the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma)—that is, when I speak of the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth as the factors of enlightenment—this is called the intrinsic characteristic (svabhāvalakṣaṇa) of those phenomena.”

It is that which, together with the mundane and supramundane, is free from the characteristics of defilement; it gives rise to the fruits of those dharmas—the mundane and supramundane virtues—and this is called its characteristic of attainment.

Mañjuśrī! That very dharma is experienced through the wisdom of liberation; it should be known, extensively explained to others, and manifested. This is called the characteristic of the manifestation that accords with that dharma.

Mañjuśrī! That very practice of the factors of enlightenment which is free from the defiled dharmas that are contrary to the path—this is to be known as the dharma that acts as an obstacle to progress. Mañjuśrī!
To cause those dharmas to arise and increase extensively is called the characteristic of conformity to those dharmas.
Mañjuśrī! That which obstructs all dharmas is called the characteristic of transgression.
“Mañjuśrī! You should know that the merit which accords with those dharmas is called the characteristic of benefit.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We pray that the World-Honored One will once again briefly explain for the sake of all bodhisattvas the meaning of the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Mātṛkā—the characteristics of the dhāraṇīs that are not shared with any of the external paths or the two vehicles.”
"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have preached the profound Dharma; the bodhisattvas have attained its profound meaning, and having attained it, they are able to enter into all Buddha-dharmas.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Listen attentively now; I shall briefly explain for you the meaning of the dhāraṇī."
“Mañjuśrī, when the bodhisattvas have heard my Dharma, they are able to grasp my intention;
having grasped my intention, they enter into my Dharma.”
What is the brief explanation of the meaning of *dhāraṇī*?

It is that which I have taught: all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśadharma*), all pure phenomena (*vyavadānadharma*), and all those phenomena are characterized by non-awakening, by lack of agency, by non-discrimination, and by selflessness; such and such are these phenomena.

I teach that there is no sensation, no volitional action, no discrimination, and no mark of self; because all things are without sensation and without the mark of self, defiled phenomena are not first defiled and later become pure, nor are pure phenomena first pure and later named defiled.

Ignorant ordinary beings, relying on this false and defiled body, cling to the notions of self and phenomena; they calculate its essential characteristics and, based on wrong views, assert the existence of a self—claiming, "I am able to see, hear, smell, taste, touch, know, eat, be defiled, and be purified"—and thus give rise to such various practices of wrong view.

If a person can thus know, in accordance with reality, the body that is free from afflictions, that person will be able to transcend all afflictions, sever all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*), and attain ultimate purity; they will obtain the unconditioned body (*asaṃskṛta-kāya*) in which no conditioned activities whatsoever exist.
"Mañjuśrī! This is called the brief explanation of the meaning of the dhāraṇī; you should know it thus.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"All phenomena are fundamentally unstained, yet later they are not pure;
this staining and this purity— these phenomena are without self.
One who stains the body perceives a self, giving rise to the notion of 'mine'."
My defilement and my purification, my views and my nourishment—
if one can understand these thus, that person is free from afflictions and attains an undefiled body; therefore, it is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!”
“What are the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s mind?
